A diesel warms up more slowly than a petrol engine, especially at idle in winter. While driving it stays at 80–95 °C.
The RPM is steady, without hunting or jerking.
Operating temperature is 80–95 °C. In winter a truck may take a long time to warm up at idle — this is normal.
The RPM is steady. With the heater on, the PTO engaged or in winter, the ECU may raise it.
With the heater or PTO on, the RPM is higher — this is normal.

Handbrake on, gearbox in P or N. Keep your hands and clothing away from the belts and the fan: the engine may start.
Don’t touch the radiator fan with your hands while the ignition is on. On many cars it can start spinning by itself, even with the engine off.
No power: check the battery and terminals
If the dashboard is completely dark, current from the battery isn’t reaching the car. Most often the terminals or a completely flat battery are to blame.
Open the hood and wiggle the battery terminals by hand. They shouldn’t be loose.
If there is white or green deposit on the terminals, remove them (negative first, then positive), clean them and put them back (positive first, then negative).
Switch on the headlights. If they don’t light or are very dim, the battery is flat: jump-start from another car or charge it.
Check the main power fuse (below).
Check the battery isolator switch — by the batteries or a button in the cab. It must be switched on.
In a 24 V system the two batteries are connected by a link cable. Check that it is intact and tight.
The battery is most likely flat
The starter doesn’t get enough current: it cranks sluggishly and the lights dim. This happens especially often in frost and with batteries older than 4–5 years.
Check the terminals: are they tight, is there any deposit?
Jump-start from another car. Red cable: your battery positive → donor positive. Black: donor negative → bare metal on your car’s engine.
Let the donor run for 5–10 minutes, then start. Crank for no longer than 10 seconds and wait 30 seconds between attempts.
If the battery goes flat overnight again, there is a current drain or the alternator isn’t charging.
Only jump-start a 24 V vehicle from a 24 V vehicle or a 24 V jump starter.
Two batteries work as a pair: if one is weak, it drags both down. Measure each one — a good one shows 12.4–12.9 V.
There’s a click, but the starter doesn’t crank
A click means the starter solenoid has engaged and the start command is getting through. Either there isn’t enough current or the starter itself is jammed.
Switch on the headlights and turn the key again. If the headlights dim a lot, the problem is the battery or terminals.
Check that the thick cable on the starter and the ground strap from the engine to the body (frame) are tight.
Try the method from the tip below.

Tap the starter housing a few times with a hammer or a tyre iron — not hard, but firmly. Then try to start. If that doesn’t help, have a helper hold the key on “Start” while you tap. If it starts, the starter is worn — repair it before it fails completely.
The starter is silent: check the lockout and the fuse
Complete silence means the start command doesn’t reach the starter. Often this is the in-gear start protection or a blown fuse.
Automatic: is the lever definitely in P? Shift to N and try again.
Manual: press the clutch all the way down. Many cars won’t start without it.
Start button: press it with the brake pedal pressed.
Check the starter fuse and relay (below). You can temporarily swap the relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.
If a key or lock symbol is flashing, the immobilizer may be blocking the start.
Check the battery isolator switch.
On some trucks the starter won’t engage if the cab isn’t locked down after tilting.
Checked everything and the starter is still silent? Tap its housing with a hammer and try again. Sometimes the solenoid contacts get burnt, and a light tap helps you get to a workshop.
Looks like the fuel pump isn’t working
When the ignition is switched on, the pump hums for 2–3 seconds and builds pressure. If it’s silent, it isn’t getting power or it has seized.
Make sure there is fuel in the tank. If the tank is almost empty, add 5–10 litres.
Check the fuel pump fuse (below).
Find the pump relay and swap it with a neighbouring one with the same marking. If the pump starts humming, replace the relay.
On many trucks the fuel is fed by a mechanical pump on the high-pressure pump. Bleed the system with the hand primer pump until it becomes firm.

Have a helper switch on the ignition while you knock with your fist or a rubber mallet on the bottom of the tank. On many cars the pump sits under the rear seat: lift the seat, open the hatch and tap the pump cover. If the pump starts humming and the car starts, it is worn — replace it soon.
Don’t hit the tank with metal objects, don’t smoke and don’t use an open flame nearby.
The pump hums, but the engine won’t start
The pump is getting power. The cause may be fuel pressure, the filter, ignition or sensors, and it can’t be found without a scanner.
Check the ECU and ignition fuses (below).
If you filled up recently, you may have got poor-quality fuel.
Don’t crank the starter for longer than 10 seconds at a time, pause for 30 seconds so you don’t drain the battery.
Oleg will run computer diagnostics on site and find the cause.
The immobilizer is blocking the start
A key or lock symbol means the car doesn’t recognise the key and won’t let it start. The engine may not start or may die after 1–2 seconds.
Try the spare key.
Replace the battery in the key fob.
Car with a Start button: hold the key fob right against the button and press it. On many cars there is an antenna there.
If you have an alarm with remote start, disarm the car again with the alarm fob.
Oleg repairs immobilizers.
Fuel is being supplied — a diagnosis is needed
The starter cranks, the pump works, the immobilizer isn’t interfering. The cause lies in the ignition, sensors or ECU, and only a scanner can show it.
See if Check Engine is on after a start attempt. If you have a scanner, read the codes and decode them on the “Error codes” tab.
If you filled up recently, you may have got poor-quality petrol.
Don’t crank the starter for longer than 10 seconds at a time, pause for 30 seconds.
Add fuel first
With an almost empty tank, especially on a slope, the pump may suck air. The fuel level sensor can also be wrong sometimes.
Add 5–10 litres.
Switch on the ignition for 3 seconds, switch it off and repeat 2–3 times — the pump will build up pressure.
After running out of fuel, a diesel must be bled with the hand primer pump.
If it still won’t start with fuel, tap “Back” and choose “Yes, there’s fuel”.
The electric car won’t switch on: check the 12 V battery
An electric car also has an ordinary 12 V battery. It powers the control units and switches on the high-voltage battery. If it is flat, the car won’t switch on even with a full traction battery.
Press the brake pedal and the Start button: READY should appear on the dashboard.
Replace the battery in the key fob or hold the fob to the backup start spot (see the owner’s manual).
Measure the 12 V battery voltage: below 12 V — charge it or connect a jump starter as described in the manual. Only connect to the 12 V system.
If the car won’t switch on with a charged 12 V battery, a diagnosis is needed.
Oleg will check the 12 V system and the control units with a scanner.
No power: battery, terminals or the main fuse
If the dash doesn’t light up at all, current from the battery isn’t reaching the motorcycle. Most often the battery is flat, the terminals have come loose or the main fuse has blown.
Remove the seat or side cover and check the battery terminals: the small bolts often work loose from vibration.
Measure the battery voltage: below 12 V, it needs charging.
Check the main fuse (below). It is often right on the starter relay, next to the battery.
Check the ignition switch and the connector under it: the dash should light up when you turn the key.

After winter a motorcycle battery is almost always flat. Charge it with a motorcycle battery charger at a low current — about a tenth of the capacity (for 8 Ah — about 0.8 A). Lithium batteries must only be charged with a charger that has a lithium mode.
A motorcycle battery is small and drains quickly: after winter, from an alarm, or if the bike has stood for a long time. The starter cranks sluggishly and the dash dims.
Measure the voltage: a charged battery shows 12.6–12.9 V (lithium — 13.0–13.4 V).
Charge the battery with a motorcycle battery charger.
You can jump-start from a car, but only with the car’s engine off: the car’s alternator can damage the motorcycle’s electronics.

With a manual gearbox you can bump-start it: 2nd gear, pull the clutch, push it up to speed and release the clutch sharply. On a fuel-injected bike this only works if the battery isn’t completely flat.
If the battery goes flat again within a couple of days, check the charging (“Sensors” tab, 5000 rpm mode).
The relay clicks, but the starter doesn’t crank
A click means the starter relay engages, but current doesn’t reach the starter. Most often it’s a weak battery, corroded terminals or burnt relay contacts.
Check and tighten the battery terminals and the thick cable on the starter.
Check the ground: the cable from the battery to the frame or engine.
Measure the voltage while pressing the starter: below 9.6 V — the battery can’t cope.
Tap the starter housing a few times with a hammer handle or a tyre iron and try again. If it starts, the starter is worn (brushes or bushings) — get it repaired.
Motorcycle in neutral and on its stand. Keep your hands away from the chain and the wheel.
The starter is silent: check the safety cut-offs
Motorcycles and scooters have many protections against accidental starting. The starter is almost always silent because of one of them, not because of a breakdown.
The engine stop switch (Run/Stop, usually red on the right handlebar) is on RUN.
Neutral: the green N light is on. Or pull the clutch all the way in.
Side stand: on many motorcycles the starter won’t engage or the engine dies if the side stand is down and a gear is engaged. Raise it.
Scooter: the starter only works with the brake held.
Check the main fuse and the starter relay (below).
The side stand sensor and the clutch switch often corrode or break. If the bike only starts in neutral or dies when you engage a gear, they are the problem.
Carburettor: check the fuel and the choke
The starter cranks but the engine won’t catch. On carburettor bikes it’s most often the fuel tap, the choke, stale petrol or a flooded spark plug.
Fuel tap on ON or RES (reserve). A vacuum tap has a PRI position — it lets fuel through without vacuum.
When cold, use the choke (CHOKE lever) and turn it off after starting.
If the bike stood all winter, the petrol may have gone stale. Drain the petrol from the float bowls via the screws at the bottom of the carburettor and fill with fresh petrol.
Unscrew the spark plug: if it’s wet and smells of petrol, it’s flooded. Dry it, crank the engine without the plug and screw it back in.
Check the spark (tip below).

Put the cap on the removed spark plug, press its thread against the engine metal and press the starter: there should be a bright blue spark. If it’s weak or absent — the plug, coil or ignition module.
Hold the spark plug with insulated pliers. There must be no spilled petrol nearby.
Looks like the fuel pump isn’t working
On a fuel-injected motorcycle the in-tank pump hums for 2–3 seconds and builds pressure when you switch on the ignition. If it’s silent, the pump isn’t getting power or it has seized.
Check the Run/Stop switch: in the STOP position the pump doesn’t switch on.
Check that there is petrol in the tank.
Check the injection and fuel pump fuse (below) and the pump relay.
Look at the pump connector on the tank: on motorcycles it often corrodes.
Switch on the ignition and tap the tank with your palm from below or from the side where the pump sits. If it starts humming, the pump is worn and needs replacing soon.
Don’t hit the tank with metal, don’t smoke nearby.
The pump works — check the spark and the error codes
Fuel is being supplied, but the engine won’t catch. The cause lies in the ignition, sensors or ECU.
Look at the dash: if the FI light is flashing or the engine symbol is on, the ECU has stored a fault. Count the flashes or read the code on the screen and enter it on the “Error codes” tab.
If the key symbol is flashing, the immobilizer may be blocking the start. Try the spare key.
Check the spark plugs and the spark.
Check the injection fuse (below).
Oleg will connect a scanner to the motorcycle and find the cause.
The battery keeps going flat: check the charging
The most common cause on motorcycles is a faulty regulator/rectifier or alternator stator. Less often a current drain (alarm, connected gadgets) or an old battery.
Start the engine and measure the battery voltage at 4000–5000 rpm with the headlight on. The norm is 13.5–14.8 V.
Below 13.5 V — not charging: the regulator/rectifier or the stator. Above 15 V — overcharging, the regulator/rectifier is faulty.
Inspect the connector between the stator and the regulator/rectifier: it often burns and melts.
If the battery is more than 3–4 years old, load-test it.
Oleg will check the stator and the regulator/rectifier and find the current drain.
Check the lights and turn signals
On a motorcycle almost all the lighting goes through the handlebar switches, and they corrode from moisture. Start with the simple things.
If one bulb doesn’t light, replace the bulb.
If nothing lights at all, check the lighting fuse (below).
If the turn signals flash very fast, a bulb has blown or LED indicators were fitted without an LED flasher relay.
If the turn signals don’t flash at all — the flasher relay. Fit an LED or a standard one, depending on your bulbs.
Flick the handlebar switches several times: if the light flickers, the contacts are corroded and need cleaning.
FI light on or an error on the dash

The motorcycle’s ECU has stored a fault. On new motorcycles (Euro 5) the codes are read with an OBD scanner, like on cars. Many Japanese motorcycles show the code as a number on the dash or by flashing the FI light.
If the code is shown as a number on the dash, write it down.
If the FI light is flashing, count the flashes: on Honda long flashes are tens, short ones are units.
Enter the code on the “Error codes” tab or take a photo of the dash.
If the light is flashing and the engine jerks or dies, don’t ride far.
Oleg will decode the code for your make and find the cause.
The engine is overheating: check the fan
On liquid-cooled motorcycles the fan switches on at about 100–105 °C. In traffic without the fan the engine overheats quickly.
Don’t open the radiator cap on a hot engine: steam and coolant will scald you.
Switch off the engine and let it cool down.
Check the coolant level in the expansion tank.
Check the fan fuse (below).
Look at the connectors of the fan and the temperature sensor.
Until it’s fixed, switch off the engine during long stops in traffic.
The electric motorcycle or scooter won’t move
Electric vehicles refuse to move because of safety cut-offs more often than because of breakdowns.
Don’t open the traction battery: high voltage and a fire risk.
Check the battery charge and that it is installed correctly and latched.
Side stand up, Run/Stop switch on RUN.
On many scooters you need to hold the brake and press a button to enter ride mode.
If the battery is completely flat, the protection may have switched it off. Charge it for a few hours with the original charger.
Look at the error code on the display and enter it on the “Error codes” tab.
Oleg will check the wiring, connectors and the control unit.
The glow plugs don’t work
A cold diesel needs glow plugs: they heat the combustion chambers before starting. If the coil symbol doesn’t come on or flashes, the plugs are most likely not heating.
Check the glow plug power fuse (below).
Find the glow plug relay or control unit and check its connector.
Check the plugs with a multimeter: a good one reads almost 0 Ω (usually under 2 Ω); an open circuit means the plug has burned out.
On many cars a flashing coil symbol means an engine fault — read the code with a scanner.
Many trucks have an intake air heater (flame or electric) instead of glow plugs. It has its own relay and power fuse.
Diesel in frost: check the fuel
Preheating works, but the engine won’t catch. In winter the cause is most often gelled summer fuel (wax) or frozen water in the filter.
Don’t heat the fuel filter, tank or lines with an open flame — that’s a fire.
Think about where you filled up. In winter you need winter or arctic diesel.
Put the vehicle in a warm garage for a few hours — the wax will melt.
Drain the water from the fuel filter/separator (the tap at the bottom of the filter).
Check the fuel filter heater (if fitted) and its fuse.
Crank the starter for no longer than 10–15 seconds, with pauses — save the battery.
Looks like there is air in the fuel system
After a filter change, running out of fuel or a long period standing, air gets into the fuel and the diesel won’t start.
Bleed the system with the hand primer pump (bulb or button on the filter) until it becomes firm.
On some vehicles you can switch on the ignition several times for 10–15 seconds — the electric lift pump will bleed the system by itself.
Check for fuel leaks at the filter and connections: air gets sucked in through them.
If it won’t start after bleeding, check the rail pressure while cranking (“Sensors” tab).
The diesel fuel system needs checking
The starter cranks, but the diesel won’t catch. The cause may be fuel pressure, injectors, sensors or the ECU.
Check that there is fuel and the filter isn’t clogged.
Drain the water from the fuel filter/separator.
If you have a scanner, check the rail pressure while cranking. Usually at least 200 bar is needed to start (“Sensors” tab).
Read the error codes and decode them on the “Error codes” tab.
Oleg will run computer diagnostics on the diesel on site.
The engine has limited its power
A diesel goes into a power limit when it detects a fault in the AdBlue (SCR) system or the particulate filter, or a threat to the engine. The error code will show the exact cause.
Check the AdBlue level and top it up if it’s low. Only use AdBlue, never water.
AdBlue freezes at −11 °C in winter: after starting, wait for the tank heater to work.
Read the error code on the dashboard or with a scanner and decode it on the “Error codes” tab.
If the particulate filter symbol is on, drive steadily on the highway for 20–30 minutes. If that doesn’t help, a forced regeneration is needed.
Oleg will read the codes with a scanner and find the cause of the power limit.
The fan isn’t supposed to spin yet
The radiator fan only switches on when the engine has warmed up to about 95–105 °C. On a cold engine it stays still — this is normal.
Check again when the needle reaches the middle or slightly above.
If the needle rises above the middle and the fan still hasn’t switched on, go back and choose the second option.
Trucks often have a viscous-clutch fan: on a cold engine it turns slowly and easily, on a hot one it engages.
Check the radiator fan fuse
The fan doesn’t switch on from temperature or from the A/C. Most likely it isn’t getting power: a fuse, relay or connector.
Switch off the engine.
Swap the fan relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.
Look at the connector on the fan motor: has it come loose, is there corrosion?
Until it’s fixed, watch the temperature needle. In traffic, turn the heater up to maximum: it will take away some of the heat.
If a viscous or electromagnetic clutch fan doesn’t spin on a hot engine, check the clutch and its connector (on the electromagnetic one).
The fan motor is fine, the control is failing
Since the fan spins with the A/C on, the motor, fuse and wiring are fine. It isn’t being switched on by temperature because of the sensor, relay or ECU.
Until it’s repaired you can drive with the A/C on — the fan will work.
Watch the temperature needle, especially in traffic jams.
Oleg will check the sensor and the fan control with a scanner.
Pull over and switch off the engine
The needle in the red zone means overheating. If you keep driving, the cylinder head may warp, and that is an expensive repair.
Don’t open the radiator or expansion tank cap on a hot engine: steam and coolant will scald you.
Stop in a safe place and switch off the engine.
Wait 30–40 minutes for the engine to cool down.
Check the coolant level in the tank. If it’s below the MIN mark, top up with coolant (in summer, water as a last resort).
Check the radiator fan fuse (below).
Don’t drive while overheating. Call Oleg out or call a tow truck.
Check the heater fuse
The heater fan is silent at all speeds. Most often the fuse has blown, the relay has failed or the motor has seized.
Turn the speed switch through all positions.
Check the heater fuse (below).
Swap the heater relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.

The heater motor is usually under the glovebox on the passenger side. Turn the heater to maximum and tap its housing from below with your palm. If it starts spinning, the brushes or bearing are worn — the motor will need replacing soon.
The heater resistor has burned out
If the heater only blows on the highest speed, the fuse and motor are fine. Speeds 1–3 go through the resistor, and it has burned out.
Until it’s replaced, use the highest speed.
The resistor is inexpensive and usually sits next to the motor under the glovebox. Get one exactly for your model.
If a new resistor burns out quickly, the motor is binding and overloading it.
Blowing cold: the cooling system is the cause
The fan works, but the air doesn’t get warm. Most often it’s low coolant, an air lock, a thermostat that doesn’t close or a clogged heater core.
With the engine cold, check the coolant level in the expansion tank.
Look at the temperature needle. If it’s below the middle after 15 minutes of driving, it’s most likely the thermostat.
Set the control to maximum heat and listen under the dashboard. On cars with climate control the flap motor should operate.
If coolant keeps disappearing, look for a leak — it can damage the engine.
Oleg repairs heating systems.
Most likely a bulb has blown
When one headlight is out, the bulb is almost always to blame. On many cars each headlight also has its own fuse.
If the headlights are xenon, don’t take them apart yourself: the ballast produces high voltage.
Remove the bulb and look at it. A broken filament or a darkened glass means the bulb has blown.
To check, swap the bulbs of the left and right headlights.
Don’t touch the glass of a new halogen bulb with your fingers — the grease will make it burn out quickly.
If the new bulb doesn’t light either, check the fuse for this headlight (below).
In a 24 V system only fit 24 V bulbs — a 12 V bulb will blow immediately.
Check the headlight fuses and relay
Both bulbs rarely blow at the same time. Usually a fuse, a relay or the stalk switch is to blame.
Check both headlight fuses, left and right (below).
Swap the headlight relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.
If low beam doesn’t work but high beam does (or vice versa), the stalk switch is often to blame.
Check the parking light fuse
Parking lights and tail lights are usually powered by one fuse. The instrument and button illumination often goes out with them.
Check the parking light fuse (below).
If one lamp is out, replace the bulb and check the socket for corrosion.
On a tractor unit, check the trailer socket and its connector: corroded contacts are a common cause.
The brake lights don’t work
When both brake lights are out, the fuse or the switch above the brake pedal is to blame.
Driving without brake lights is dangerous: drivers behind can’t see you braking.
Check the brake light fuse (below).
Look at the switch above the brake pedal: is the stop broken, has the connector come off?
On trucks with air brakes the brake lights are switched by a pressure switch — check it and its connector.
Check the power window fuse
All the motors rarely fail at once. Look for a common cause.
Check the window lock button on the driver’s door: is it pressed?
Check the power window fuse (below).
Swap the power window relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.
One window doesn’t work
The fuse usually has nothing to do with it. The cause is the switch, the motor, the regulator or the wires in the rubber boot between the door and the body.
Press the switch and listen. If the motor hums but the window doesn’t move, the cable or regulator is broken.
If there’s complete silence, try raising this window with the switch on the driver’s door. If it works from there, the switch on this door is broken.
While holding the switch, tap the door panel with your palm. If the window moves, the motor brushes are worn.
Open the door and look at the rubber boot with the wires: the wires often break there.
Check the central locking
First work out where the fault is: in the key fob or in the lock itself.
Lock with the button inside the cabin or with the key in the door. If that works, the problem is the key fob: replace its battery.
If nothing works, check the central locking fuse (below).
If one door doesn’t work, it’s most likely the lock actuator in that door or the wires in the rubber boot.
Check the cigarette lighter fuse
This fuse blows often: from a faulty charger, a coin or a paper clip in the socket.
Try the charger in another car: maybe it’s the charger that’s broken.
Shine a light into the socket: is there any debris or a coin?
Check the fuse (below). On many cars it also powers the radio.
If it blows again, don’t fit a higher rating: there is a short in the socket.
In a 24 V system the cigarette lighter socket is often 24 V too. A 12 V charger may burn out — check the label on the charger.
The light means the engine control unit has stored a fault. You can’t find the cause without a scanner: it could be a cheap sensor or a serious failure.
If the light is flashing and the engine is misfiring, reduce the load and don’t drive far — you can ruin the catalytic converter.
If it’s on steadily and the car drives as usual, you can calmly drive to a workshop.
If you have an error code, decode it on the “Error codes” tab.
Check the fuel cap. On some cars the light comes on if it isn’t closed tightly.
On a truck the code may be in SPN and FMI format — you can decode that on the “Error codes” tab too.

The battery drains by itself
Usually it’s one of three causes: a current drain, the alternator isn’t charging, or the battery has reached the end of its life.
Check whether a light stays on in the trunk, glovebox or cabin when the car is locked.
If you have a voltmeter, measure at the terminals. Engine off and battery charged: about 12.6 V. Engine running: 13.5–14.8 V.
Below 13.5 V with the engine running — suspect the alternator.
If the battery is more than 4–5 years old, load-test it.
For a 24 V system: engine off — about 25 V, engine running — 27.2–28.8 V.
When parked, switch off the battery isolator — the batteries drain less.
Oleg will find the current drain: he will measure the consumption and use the fuses to work out which circuit is draining the battery.

How an error code is structured
Cars and light trucks (OBD-II).

A code made of a letter and four characters, for example P0301. The letter is the system: P — engine and transmission, C — chassis (ABS, ESP), B — body (airbags, climate, lights), U — communication between control units. The digit after the letter: 0 and 2 — a generic code, the same for all makes; 1 — a manufacturer code.
Trucks and buses (J1939).

A code made of two numbers: SPN — which parameter or sensor, FMI — what is wrong with it (above normal, open circuit, short, etc.). For example, SPN 110 FMI 0 means engine coolant temperature above normal.
Some engines (Cummins on KAMAZ, MAN, Volvo) also show their own fault numbers. If the code is in a different format, send it to Oleg.
Motorcycles.

New motorcycles (Euro 5) have OBD-II codes, like cars. Many Japanese motorcycles show their own code as a number on the dash or by flashing the FI light: on Honda long flashes are tens, short ones are units. Oleg can add such codes to the reference for your make.
Write down the codes before clearing them. Clearing a code doesn’t mean fixing it: if the cause is still there, it will come back.

How to measure correctly
Connect a scanner to the OBD port under the steering wheel: an ELM327 adapter with a phone app or a professional scanner.
Open “Live data” and select the parameters you need.
Set up the mode conditions: warm up the engine, switch off the headlights, heater and A/C, hold the RPM steady.
Watch for 20–30 seconds. If the value jumps, enter the average.
Compare the modes with each other. The difference between idle and raised RPM often points to the cause better than a single reading.
Don’t look at your phone while driving. Have a passenger take readings on the move, or record the scanner screen on video.

Outboard starter won’t crank: kill switch, neutral, battery
If the starter is silent or only clicks, most often the kill switch clip isn’t in place, the throttle lever isn’t in neutral or the battery is flat.
Check the kill switch clip on the lanyard: it must be in place in the switch on the remote control or the motor.
Put the throttle and shift lever in neutral: the motor won’t start in gear.
Check the battery terminals: water makes them corrode. Clean and tighten them.
Measure the battery: below 12.4 V — charge it.
Check the fuse next to the starter relay on the motor or in the remote control (below).
The relay clicks but the starter doesn’t crank — check the heavy cable on the starter and the ground.
Flat battery? Many electric-start motors can be started with the emergency starter rope. It comes with the motor and is wound around the flywheel under the cowling. See the motor’s manual for how.
Fuel isn’t reaching the motor
If the bulb stays soft, fuel isn’t flowing: the tank vent is closed, the hose connector isn’t clicked in, or air is getting in.
Open the air vent on the fuel tank cap — otherwise fuel won’t flow.
Check the fuel hose connectors on the tank and the motor: push them in until they click.
Squeeze the bulb (arrow toward the motor) until it gets firm.
The bulb never gets firm — the hose is cracked or the bulb’s valves have failed. Replace the bulb.
Old fuel or fuel with water — drain it and fill with fresh. For a two-stroke motor, mix in oil at the right ratio.
Fuel is getting through: check the choke and spark plugs
A firm bulb means fuel is getting through. The motor usually won’t catch because of the choke or flooded or fouled spark plugs.
Cold carburetted motor: pull out the choke, start it and ease the choke back in.
If you’ve been pulling for a long time, the plugs may be flooded. Remove them, dry them, turn the motor over 5–6 times without plugs and refit them.
A plug that is black, sooty or wet with oil — replace it. On two-stroke motors plugs are replaced often.
Check the plug caps: pushed on until they click, no cracks.
Is the kill switch clip in place? Without it there’s no spark, even if the motor turns over.
A fuel-injected motor won’t start — read the error codes with a scanner or send a description to Oleg.
No telltale water stream — shut the motor off
A stream of water should always come out of the hole on the side of the motor. No stream means water isn’t cooling the motor, and it can overheat within minutes.
Never run the motor without water, even on shore: the water pump impeller will burn out in seconds.
Shut the motor off.
Clear the telltale hole with a thin wire — it often clogs with sand.
Inspect the water intake on the motor’s lower unit: remove weeds, plastic bags, silt.
Start it again. Still no stream — the water pump impeller is most likely worn. It is replaced every 1–2 seasons.
If the motor beeps or the overheat light is on, don’t keep going until it’s repaired.
Oleg or a marine mechanic will replace the impeller and check the thermostat.
Motor beeping: overheating, oil or water in the fuel
An alarm on an outboard most often means overheating, low oil or water in the fuel. The motor may reduce its own revs.
Throttle back and check the telltale water stream. No stream — shut the motor off and see the cooling tip.
Four-stroke motor: check the oil level in the crankcase with the dipstick.
Two-stroke motor with oil injection: check the oil in the tank.
Drain water from the fuel/water separator filter, if fitted.
The alarm doesn’t go away — read the error codes with a scanner or send a description to Oleg.
Trim not working: check the fuse and relays
The trim raises and lowers the motor. If the trim motor is silent, the fuse, a relay or a corroded switch connector is usually to blame.
Check the trim fuse (below).
There are two trim relays: up and down. If it only works one way, swap them. If the fault moves to the other direction, replace the relay.
Check the trim switch connector on the throttle handle: corrosion from water is a common cause.
The trim motor hums but the outboard doesn’t move — check the oil level in the trim reservoir.
You can lower the motor by hand by opening the manual release valve 2–3 turns — see the manual. Then close it again.
The boat battery isn’t charging
The motor charges the battery only above idle. Small pull-start motors may have no charging at all.
Check the battery terminals and cables: corrosion from water prevents charging.
Measure the voltage with the motor running at medium revs: 13.5–14.5 V means it’s charging.
Around 12 V — check the charging fuse and the rectifier/regulator connectors on the motor.
Battery goes flat overnight — when moored, turn off the battery switch or disconnect a terminal.
On a boat, lights usually fail because of corroded connectors or a blown fuse.
Check the lights fuse on the switch panel or near the battery.
Inspect the bulb and socket: green deposits — clean them off.
Wire connectors at the bow and stern are a common cause: disconnect, clean and coat with silicone grease.
Fit bulbs of the same voltage — usually 12 V.
For a four-stroke motor — every 100 engine hours or once a season. For a two-stroke, oil is mixed into the fuel or added to the oil tank.
Gear oil in the lower unit

How to choose
How to choose oil viscosity

What matters most is the temperature where you drive, not the car’s mileage. The hotter it is, the higher the viscosity should be: on a hot engine, thicker oil keeps its film and protects the engine better.
The second number is for heat.
The first number is for cold starts.
Summer and winter can differ.
If winters are cold and summers are hot, use a wide-range oil such as 5W‑40, or switch viscosity with the season.
Stay within what your owner’s manual allows: in some modern engines designed for 0W‑16 and 0W‑20, oil that is too thick interferes with the variable valve timing.

It is the viscosity on a warmed-up engine. In summers up to +25 °C, 30 is enough; up to +35 °C, use 40; in heat above +35 °C, in traffic jams and under heavy load, use 50. For example, 5W‑40 instead of 5W‑30.
The lower it is, the easier the engine starts in frost: 0W — down to about −35 °C, 5W — to −30 °C, 10W — to −25 °C, 15W — to −20 °C.

Automatic gearbox: stuck in P or won’t shift
Gearbox problem
What’s happening with the gearbox?
The lever won’t move out of P (park)
The lever moves, but the car won’t drive
Stuck in one gear, won’t shift, jerks
Gearbox light or AT error on the dashboard
Brake lights when pressing the brake
Press the brake pedal and ask someone to look from behind — or check the reflection in a window or shop front.
Do the brake lights come on?
Yes, they light up
No, they don’t
I can’t check
How the selector lever moves
How does the selector lever move?
Too easily, with no effort or clicks
As usual, with clicks
Unlock the lever with the Shift Lock button

Automatic gearboxes have an emergency lever release: a button or a slot under a small cover next to the selector (marked Shift Lock or Shift Release). Use it when the lever won’t move out of P: a flat battery, a faulty brake pedal switch or a faulty lock.
Only release the lever with the car standing still: apply the handbrake and hold the brake pedal.
Apply the handbrake, switch off the engine, press and hold the brake pedal.
Find the button or the small cover marked Shift Lock next to the lever. Carefully pry the cover off with a screwdriver.
Press into the slot with the key or a screwdriver and, while holding it, move the lever to N. Then start the engine.
Dashboard dim or dark — jump-start or charge the battery first: without power the lock won’t release the lever.
Check that the brake lights work. If not — the brake light fuse (below) or the switch above the brake pedal.
If the lever won’t leave P even with the Shift Lock button, the lock or the switch needs repair. Oleg will come and sort it out.
The brake lights are out — that’s why the lever won’t leave P

The gearbox releases the lever from P only when it “sees” the brake pressed. The signal comes from the same switch above the brake pedal that turns on the brake lights. No brake lights — the unit doesn’t see the brake and keeps the lever locked.
Driving without brake lights is dangerous: drivers behind can’t see you braking. Fix them before you drive.
Check the brake light fuse (below). If it’s blown, replace it with one of the same rating.
Look at the switch above the brake pedal: is the stop broken, has the switch fallen out, is the connector loose?
Need to move the car now — release the lever with the Shift Lock button: handbrake on, brake pedal pressed, press into the slot by the lever and move it to N.
Oleg will check the switch, the brake light wiring and the selector lock.
The selector cable has probably come off or snapped

The lever in the cabin is connected to the gearbox by a cable. When the cable comes off the lever on the gearbox (often the plastic bushing of the end crumbles) or snaps, the lever moves easily with no detents, and the gear in the gearbox itself doesn’t change.
Until the cable is fixed, P may not engage — always use the handbrake.
Look at the dashboard: if the gear letter doesn’t change, or changes but the car won’t drive, it’s most likely the cable.
Under the hood, find the lever on the gearbox where the cable connects: has the end come off, is the bushing intact?
If the end came off and the bushing is intact, push it back on until it clicks.
If the bushing crumbled or the cable snapped, call a technician: a bushing or cable is replaced quickly.
Oleg will come, fit a new bushing or cable and check that the lever and gearbox positions match.
The cable is in place, but the car won’t drive forward or backward, or only in one direction. Most often the gearbox is low on fluid or has an internal fault.
Don’t rev the engine or rock the car — you can damage the gearbox for good.
See if the gearbox light or Check Engine is on and decode the code in the “Error codes” tab.
A puddle of red or brown oil under the car means a gearbox leak. Don’t drive any further.
Check the gearbox fluid level if it has a dipstick — strictly as the manual says (usually with a warm engine, lever in P).
Call a tow truck or a technician.
Oleg will read the gearbox codes with a scanner and tell you whether it needs repair.
The gearbox is in limp mode

When the gearbox control unit detects a fault, it switches to limp mode: the car drives in one gear (often 2nd or 3rd), doesn’t shift, and D engages with a jolt. This is how the gearbox protects itself.
Stop, switch off the engine for 1–2 minutes and start again — sometimes the mode resets until the next fault.

If the key battery is dead on a VW with a start button: on models with a slot, insert the key into the slot and press it like a button while holding the brake. The first warning comes at 1,500 miles (~2,400 km) of range, the second with a chime at 500 miles (~800 km); if you drive past the shown range, the engine won’t start. When the tank is empty a chime sounds, and after you stop, the engine won’t start again. A full tank lasts about 9,000 miles (~14,500 km).

Stage 1: the DEF light is on — low level. Stage 2: DEF + Check Engine — even lower level, wrong DEF or SCR fault, slight power loss. Stage 3: DEF almost empty, wrong DEF or an SCR fault lasting over 5 hours — the DEF light flashes, major power loss. Stage 4: + red Stop Engine after refuelling without adding DEF, an hour of idling or a stop — speed limited to 5 mph (~8 km/h); since 2026 Cummins has been releasing US software updates with a final stage of 25 mph. What to do: fill DEF to ISO 22241; if the lights stay on, go to a repair shop straight away.

Euro 5: the light comes on at 10% AdBlue; if the SCR isn’t working, power drops by 25–40% depending on vehicle weight, and even more with an empty tank, until you refill. Euro 6: if you ignore the warning, according to Scania, after 10 engine hours speed is limited to 20 km/h (“creep mode”); on Iveco creep mode starts at a 5% level.

Idle speed hunts or the engine runs rough at idle
Idle speed hunts
Idle hunting: check for a vacuum leak

A common cause of a rough idle is a vacuum leak: extra air gets into the intake bypassing the mass air flow sensor (MAF) or downstream of the throttle — through a cracked intake hose, a vacuum line, the intake manifold gasket or the PCV valve. Signs: the idle hunts or jumps, the engine runs rough at idle, and lean codes P0171 and P0174 may set.

Carburetor cleaner is flammable. Spray in short, small bursts and only on cool parts of the intake — never on the exhaust manifold, ignition coils or plug wires. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby, don’t smoke, and don’t work in a closed garage.

Connect a scan tool and find intake manifold pressure (the MAP sensor). With the engine off and the ignition on it equals atmospheric pressure — about 900 mbar (90 kPa). The exact figure depends on where you are: the higher above sea level, the lower it is.

Start the engine and let it warm up. At idle intake pressure drops to roughly 300–400 mbar (30–40 kPa). Noticeably higher and wandering — suspect a vacuum leak; misfires or off timing can look the same.
Check the fuel trims: on a warm idle the sum of short- and long-term trim goes above +10…+15 % and drops at higher rpm — the typical picture of a vacuum leak.
A smoke machine finds the leak most precisely: smoke is fed into the intake and comes out wherever it isn’t sealed.

Without a smoke machine: with the engine running, lightly spray carburetor cleaner along the intake joints — from the MAF along the hose to the throttle body, along the intake manifold gasket and the vacuum lines. If the rpm rises for a moment, the leak is near that spot.
Check the obvious: clamps and the intake boot after the MAF, vacuum lines (cracks, popped-off hoses), the brake booster hose, the PCV valve, the oil filler cap and the dipstick.

I check for a vacuum leak with the scan tool first: with the engine off intake pressure is about 900 — that’s atmospheric; with it running, 300–400. If it’s higher at idle, I look for the leak with a smoke machine, and if I don’t have one handy I lightly spray carb cleaner along the intake from the MAF. If the rpm picks up, the leak is roughly there.
Oleg will smoke-test the intake, find the leak and fix it. Mobile service available.

Gearbox slipping: revs rise but the car doesn’t move

The engine revs up but the car accelerates sluggishly or doesn’t move, and revs flare during shifts — that’s the gearbox slipping. It’s a fault in the gearbox itself: most often worn clutch packs inside or low fluid.
Don’t floor it to “get through”: slipping burns the clutches in minutes and makes the repair pricier. If it slips badly, call a tow truck.
Look under the car: a puddle of red or brown fluid means a gearbox leak — don’t drive on.
If the gearbox has a dipstick, check the fluid level and condition strictly per the manual (usually engine warm, lever in P). Dark fluid that smells burnt means burnt clutches.
See whether the gearbox light or Check Engine is on and decode the code in the “Error codes” tab. Slipping is usually logged as P0730–P0736 (incorrect gear ratio).
Fluid is fine but it still slips — internal wear: clutch packs, valve body. That’s a gearbox rebuild: go to automatic transmission specialists, not auto electricians.

If the engine revs but the car won’t go, it’s the gearbox hardware itself — the clutch packs. That’s not for electricians but for transmission shops that rebuild automatics. Before that you can check the fluid and read the codes so you arrive with a diagnosis.
Internal gearbox repair is done by automatic transmission specialists, not auto electricians. Oleg can read the gearbox codes with a scanner beforehand so you arrive with a ready diagnosis.
Kicks and jerks when shifting
Jolts when shifting or when selecting D and R come from a fault the gearbox control unit sees, from lost adaptations, or from the fluid: low, old or the wrong spec.
Run a diagnosis: read the gearbox codes with a scanner and decode them in the “Error codes” tab. Gearbox codes are usually P07xx.

No codes — one option is a gearbox adaptation: the learned values are reset with a scanner and the gearbox re-learns around the wear. Then drive calmly so it can “learn”; each gearbox has its own procedure.
Check the fluid: level, colour and smell, strictly per the manual. Low or old fluid also causes incorrect shifting. Use only fluid with the spec listed for your gearbox.
Check the battery and terminals: voltage dips make the gearbox control unit shift harshly.
If the kicks remain after adaptation and a fluid change, the gearbox needs repair at a transmission shop.
If the gearbox kicks, the first thing I do is a diagnosis. No codes — one option is an adaptation. And I always check the fluid: it can also cause incorrect shifting.
Oleg will run a scanner diagnosis of the gearbox and, if there are no codes, an adaptation. If the cause is inside the gearbox, he’ll tell you where to go.
The car goes forward but not in reverse, or the other way round. That means the fault is inside the gearbox itself: a worn or broken clutch pack, brake band or valve-body valve for that gear.
Don’t try to “force” the gear with throttle — you can finish the gearbox off.
Look at the dash: does the letter change to R (or D)? If not, first check the selector cable, as in “The lever moves but the car doesn’t go”.
If the gearbox has a dipstick, check the fluid level per the manual. A puddle of fluid under the car — don’t drive on.
Check the gearbox error code and decode it in the “Error codes” tab.
This is an internal gearbox repair: go to automatic transmission specialists, not auto electricians. Get there on a tow truck.
If the car only goes forward and not in reverse, or the other way round, the problem is in the gearbox itself. That’s a job for transmission shops that repair automatics, not electricians.
Repairs are done by automatic transmission specialists. Oleg can read the gearbox codes before the repair.

To get going I press the shift-lock release — it’s usually under a little cap near the selector. Then I check the fuses: the brake lights may be out. If the fuse is fine, I check the brake pedal switch.
First I check the brake-light fuse, then the brake pedal switch — it often breaks or falls out. To get going right now, use the shift-lock release under the cap by the selector.
Starter keeps cranking after start
Check Engine flashes, engine misfires
Starter keeps cranking after you release the key

You released the key (or the Start button) but the starter keeps cranking or whines with the engine running. This happens when the starter solenoid contacts stick, or when the starter’s thin wire keeps getting power — from the ignition switch, the starter relay or the wiring.
A starter that won’t disengage overheats in a minute or two, can melt the wiring and damage the flywheel ring gear. Shut the engine off at once and disconnect the battery’s negative terminal.
Turn the engine off and disconnect the battery’s negative terminal — the starter will stop.
Find the thin wire on the starter (the control wire on the solenoid) and disconnect it. Insulate its end so it can’t touch metal. Leave the thick power cable alone.

Reconnect the negative terminal. If the starter cranks again even with the thin wire off, the problem is the starter itself: the solenoid contacts are stuck. Disconnect the terminal again — the starter needs repair or replacing.

If the starter no longer cranks, the problem is the wiring: the thin wire is getting constant power. Check the starter relay (you can swap it with an identical relay in the box), the ignition switch contacts and the wire from the switch to the starter.
Don’t start the car until the cause is found: the starter may stay engaged again.
If the starter keeps cranking after the ignition key is released, I disconnect the thin wire from the starter. Still cranking — it’s the starter. Stopped — it’s the wiring, and I trace the circuit.
Oleg will find where the starter’s power comes from — relay, ignition switch or wiring — or remove the starter for repair. Call-outs available.
Flashing Check Engine: misfires

If Check Engine flashes erratically at start-up or while driving and the engine runs rough, those are misfires: the mixture isn’t igniting in a cylinder. The usual culprits are spark plugs, plug boots or ignition coils.
While the light flashes, go easy on the throttle and don’t drive far: unburnt fuel gets into the exhaust and can ruin the catalytic converter quickly.
Read the error code: P0300 means random misfires, P0301–P0308 a specific cylinder (the last digit is the cylinder number). Decode it in the “Error codes” tab.
Turn the engine off and inspect the coils and boots: cracks, arcing marks (white or dark tracks), oil in the plug wells, corroded connectors.
Remove the plugs: black soot, oil, a cracked insulator, a wide gap or a worn electrode — replace the plugs as a set.
Coil test: swap the coil from the misfiring cylinder with a neighbouring one. If the misfire “moves” to the other cylinder, the coil is bad. If it stays put, check the plug, injector and compression.
If misfires began after rain or an engine wash, dry out the plug wells and boots.

If Check Engine starts flashing erratically when the engine starts, it’s mostly misfires: plugs, boots or coils. I start with the error code — it points to the cylinder — then check the plug and swap the coils.
Oleg will read the codes, find the misfiring cylinder and check the plugs, boots and coils. Call-outs available.

Panel gaps around doors, bonnet and wings are even on both sides
Uneven gaps and mismatched panel shades are signs of accident repair.
Factory paint: the thickness gauge shows no filler or repaint
Factory paint is usually around 80–150 µm. Much more means repaint or filler.
No rust or rot on the sills, wheel arches and underbody
The glass is all from one maker and one year
The marking is in the corner of the glass. One replaced windscreen is fine; several replaced windows are a question for the seller.
No signs of water in the cabin and boot
Lift the mats and boot lining: damp, silt, rust on the seat mounts and a mouldy smell are signs of a flood car.
With the ignition on all dash warning lights come on, then go out after start
Check Engine, airbags (SRS), ABS, oil and battery should light for 2–3 seconds. If one doesn’t, it may have been disconnected to hide a fault.
After start no warning light stays on
Battery voltage with the engine off is 12.4–12.7 V
Measure at the terminals with a multimeter before starting. Below 12.2 V the battery is flat or worn.
With the engine running the voltage is 13.8–14.7 V
That means the alternator is charging. Switch on the lights and heater — the voltage shouldn’t drop below 13.5 V.
The starter spins briskly and the engine starts first time
Lights, indicators, brake lights, windows, central locking, heater and air con all work
The wiring shows no tampering: twisted joints, tape, extra wires
Look under the dash and bonnet. Twisted joints cause future faults and current drains.
Cold start is smooth: no knocking, blue or black smoke
Ask the seller not to warm the engine before you arrive. Touch the bonnet — it should be cold.
No oil or coolant leaks, the engine is dry
No emulsion (white sludge) under the oil filler cap
Emulsion means coolant is getting into the oil: often a blown head gasket.
Oil and coolant level and colour are normal
Idle is steady and the engine doesn’t misfire
The scanner shows no codes in the modules: engine, gearbox, ABS, airbags
Scan all modules, not just the engine.
Readiness monitors are complete — codes weren’t cleared before the sale
If codes were cleared recently, some monitors will show “not ready”. That’s sometimes how faults are hidden.
The mileage stored in the modules matches the odometer
In many cars other modules store mileage too — engine, gearbox, ABS. A mismatch points to rollback.
Sensor readings are normal: fuel trims, temperature, voltage
Compare with the reference in the “Sensors” section.
The gearbox shifts smoothly, without kicks or slipping
The car doesn’t pull to one side, the steering wheel is straight
Brakes without judder or squeal
No suspension knocks over bumps
No new codes or overheating after the drive

Scanner can’t see the car
The scanner won’t connect: “no communication with the module”. Usually there’s no power at the OBD socket, the CAN bus is open or shorted, or the adapter doesn’t support the car’s protocol.
Open the OBD connector pinout — button below — and check power, ground and the CAN bus step by step with a multimeter.
First check the cigarette lighter fuse: the OBD socket is often powered from it.
Oleg will check the socket and CAN bus, find the module or device blocking communication and fix the wiring.

Switch on the ignition (no need to start the engine) and choose your make or protocol in the scanner. Cheap ELM327 adapters don’t support every protocol and module.
Check power: between pins 16 and 4 (or 5) there should be 12–14 V, 24–28 V on a truck. No voltage — most often the cigarette lighter or OBD socket fuse has blown: they’re often shared.
Check ground: resistance between pins 4, 5 and the body should be about 0 Ω.

CAN bus: switch off the ignition and measure resistance between pins 6 and 14. Normal is about 60 Ω: two 120 Ω resistors at the bus ends. 120 Ω — one branch is open or a resistor is missing; about 0 — a short; infinite — an open circuit.
With the ignition on, pin 6 (CAN High) usually reads about 2.5–3.5 V and pin 14 (CAN Low) about 1.5–2.5 V to ground.
K-line (pin 7): about 12 V at rest. Zero or a constant 5 V means a module or the alarm is pulling the line down.
Power and bus are fine but still no communication — disconnect the alarm, GPS tracker and other devices on the OBD or CAN. A faulty module can also bring the bus down: unplug modules one at a time.
The engine is short of oil pressure. Even a few minutes of driving can seize it.
Stop at once and switch off the engine.
After 5–10 minutes check the oil level with the dipstick. If low, top up and look for leaks.
Level is fine but the light is on — don’t start: call a mechanic or tow truck. It may be the sensor, but don’t risk the engine without checking.
Engine overheating
The coolant temperature is too high.
Stop and switch off the engine. Open the hood, but don’t open the expansion tank cap on a hot engine — steam will scald you.
Once it cools, check the coolant level and whether the radiator fan spins.
Battery charging
The alternator isn’t charging the battery: the car is running on the battery’s reserve and may soon stall.
Switch off everything you don’t need: heater, heated seats, music — you’ll get further.
Check the alternator belt: is it broken or slipping?
Drive to a mechanic straight away and don’t switch off on the way — it may not restart.
The parking brake is on, brake fluid is low or the brakes are faulty.
Check the parking brake is released.
Released but the light is on — check the brake fluid level in the reservoir. Below MIN — don’t drive on: there may be a leak.
A fault in the airbag system: they may not deploy in a crash.
You can drive, but don’t put off the repair.
Common causes are the connectors under the seats, the steering wheel clock spring and belt buckles. Touch connectors only with the battery terminal disconnected.
It needs a diagnosis: the code will show which circuit.
Power steering (EPS)
The electric power steering is faulty: the steering may become heavy.
If the steering is heavy, drive slowly and carefully.
Switch the engine off and restart: after a voltage dip the fault sometimes clears.
Check the battery and terminals: low voltage switches the assist off.
Immobilizer
A key or car-with-lock symbol on or flashing means the immobilizer doesn’t recognise the key and won’t let the engine start.
Flashing with the ignition off is normal: the security is armed.
On and the engine won’t start — try the spare key and replace the key battery.
Door, hood or trunk open
On with the doors closed — check the door switches: they can drain the battery.
Shut all doors, the hood and the trunk firmly.
If it stays on, the switch or its wire is faulty.
Seat belt
Someone isn’t buckled up.
Buckle up. On with the belt fastened — the buckle sensor is faulty.
Check Engine
The engine control unit has logged a fault. Steady — you can drive to a repair shop. Flashing — misfires.
Steady and the car drives normally — get to a repair shop and read the code.
Flashing and the engine misfires — ease off and don’t drive far: you can ruin the catalytic converter.
Check the fuel cap is tight.
ABS
The anti-lock system is off. The brakes work, but the wheels may lock under hard braking.
Brake early and gently, especially on slippery roads.
A common cause is a wheel speed sensor or its wire at the hub. It needs a diagnosis.
Stability control (ESP)
Flashing on a slippery road means the system is working — that’s normal. Steady means it’s off or faulty.
Steady — check the ESP off button isn’t pressed.
ABS and ESP often come on together: one cause — a wheel sensor.
Pressure has dropped in one of the tires.
Check the pressure in all wheels and inflate to the label on the door pillar.
After inflating, many cars need the system reset with a button or in the menu.
Glow plugs (diesel)
On after ignition-on means the plugs are warming the engine: wait until it goes out, then start. Flashing while driving means a fault.
Switch on the ignition, wait for the coil symbol to go out, and only then crank.
Flashing or won’t go out — check the plugs and glow relay.
Particulate filter (DPF)
The filter is clogged with soot and needs cleaning — a regeneration.
If you can, drive 15–20 minutes on the highway at a steady speed — the filter often regenerates by itself.
If that doesn’t help or power drops, a forced regeneration with a scanner is needed.
Low AdBlue or an SCR system fault. After a while the car will limit power.
Top up AdBlue: the fault often clears after topping up and driving.
Level is fine but the fault stays — the system needs a diagnosis.
The transmission control unit found a fault or the transmission overheated.
Stop, let the transmission cool and restart.
Stuck in one gear — that’s limp mode: drive calmly to a repair shop.
Water in fuel (diesel)
Water has collected in the fuel filter.
Drain the sediment through the tap at the bottom of the fuel filter-separator as described in the manual.
If it comes on again, you filled up with poor fuel: replace the filter.
The pads have worn down to the wear sensor.
Replace the pads soon, or the brake disc will start to wear.
There’s fuel left for a few dozen kilometres.
Fill up soon. Don’t keep driving on the reserve light: the fuel pump is cooled by fuel and wears faster.
Service due
This is a scheduled maintenance reminder, not a fault.
Log the service in the “Maintenance” section — the app will remind you of the next one.
High beam
High beam is on.
Switch to low beam for oncoming traffic.
Fog lights
The fog lights are on.
Switch them off in clear weather — they dazzle oncoming drivers.
Cruise control
Cruise control is on and holding the speed.
Pressing the brake or clutch switches cruise off.
The VIN plate under the windscreen matches the registration
The VIN plate or sticker is visible from outside through the windscreen, bottom left. A duplicate sticker is often on the door pillar. A re-stuck or damaged sticker is a warning sign.
The number stamped on the body matches the registration, with no signs of re-stamping
The stamping is usually on the engine bay bulkhead, under the mat by the front seat or on a pillar. Uneven digits, welding, filler or fresh paint around it — walk away.
The VIN read by the scanner from the control unit matches the registration
The scanner reads the VIN stored in the engine control unit (mode 09 in OBD). A different VIN or none means the unit was replaced: ask the seller why.

On a flat, straight road the car keeps going straight when you lightly let go of the wheel — no pull to either side

Find a flat, straight stretch with no ruts or slope and no traffic nearby. First make sure the tire pressures are equal. At 40–60 km/h, lightly let go of the wheel for a couple of seconds, keeping your hands close. The car should track straight and the wheel should stay centered. If it pulls left or right, the body geometry may be off after a crash or the wheel alignment may be out: have it checked on an alignment rack.
The mileage matches the engine hours (mostly on trucks and heavy equipment)

Engine hours are stored in the engine ECU, and they are usually not reset when the odometer is rolled back. Scan tools mostly show them on trucks and heavy equipment; few cars have this: no engine hours — skip this item. Approximate mileage = engine hours × average speed. For example, 10,000 engine hours on a long-haul tractor is roughly 400,000–600,000 km. Much less on the odometer — the mileage has most likely been rolled back.
The starter cranks, but the dash stays dark and the fuses are fine. The culprit was the ignition switch contact group — after replacing it, the car started.
Check Engine on: P0328 (knock sensor) and P0350 (coil circuit). The codes showed where to look — coils, plugs, wiring and the sensor — not what to replace right away.
The engine runs rough, code 31 — mass airflow sensor circuit. We checked the sensor connector and power; after the airflow sensor was replaced, Check Engine went out on its own.
Jerks while driving, Check Engine comes and goes: codes 19 and 14. An intermittent fault is caught by re-scanning when the jerks happen — no parts were swapped blindly.
The starter won’t crank, yet the interior lights don’t dim. The battery dropped to 9 V — we jump-started it. Bright lights don’t mean the battery is good.
Check Engine: P0421 and P0431 — the catalytic converters. The owner suspected the oxygen sensors, but these codes don’t confirm a sensor fault: the converters and exhaust are checked first.
ABS light on, turn signals, hazards and brake lights dead, the scan tool can’t see the ABS module (U0121). One of the ABS power wires had no voltage — with power supplied, the module came online.
Won’t start, P0343 and P0336 stored. After clearing, the codes didn’t come back. The fuel pump was getting power but not running — the pump and filter were replaced.
The battery was down to 3 V. After replacing it, we checked the parasitic draw — 10 mA, normal — and charging — 14.1 V under load. Only the old battery was to blame.
After suspension work, the ABS light comes on now and then: C1414 — front left wheel speed sensor. The sensor was removed and cleaned; an intermittent code is checked again when it shows up.

Won’t start and the key fob is dead: the fob battery was flat and the car battery was down to 2 V. We cleaned the terminals and jump-started it; after a discharge like that, the battery is best replaced before winter.
Won’t start, code P1200 — fuel pump circuit. The pump gets power, but it only ran after a light tap on the module cover — the pump needs replacing.
After throttle body cleaning, the idle stays around 1500 rpm. No codes, no vacuum leak — a throttle adaptation and idle relearn fixed it.
The 4WD light blinks, the instrument lights are off, 3 of 4 parking sensors don’t work. The instrument lights had simply been turned down with the dimmer.
The right turn signal flashes once and goes out; replacing the relay didn’t help. Wires left from a removed alarm were shorting to the body over bumps.
The engine ECU was faulty. A unit with the same part numbers was matched and paired to the factory immobilizer with a scan tool — about 35 minutes, and the car started.
The right turn signal stays on all the time; the hazard switch makes no difference. Unplugging the alarm connectors under the dash brought the turn signal back to normal.
Misfiring and stalling; the owner had already replaced the idle air control valve. Carb cleaner near the intake manifold smoothed the idle — a vacuum leak.
Won’t start, no sound from the fuel pump. The fuse and relay are fine, power reaches the pump module — the positive terminal on the module itself had burned.
Turn signals: bulb, relay or alarm

A turn signal flashing fast usually means a blown bulb on that side. Nothing flashes, not even the hazards — the fuse or flasher relay. One side stays on or flashes once and goes out — often an installed or removed alarm is to blame: its module and wires are tied into the turn signal circuits.

Don’t rush to replace the flasher relay blindly. On a Lexus ES300 the relay had already been replaced, but wires from a removed alarm were to blame. On a Toyota Highlander the right turn signal stayed on — unplugging the alarm connectors fixed it.
Oleg will find where the turn signal circuit drops out or shorts and properly disconnect leftover alarm wiring. Mobile service available.
Switch on the hazards. All turn signals flash — the relay and power are fine: look on the side that doesn’t work — bulb, connector, turn signal stalk.
One side flashes fast — a bulb has blown at the front, rear or in the side repeater on the fender. LED bulbs fitted without a load resistor flash the same way.

Nothing flashes, not even the hazards — check the turn signal and hazard fuse (below) and the flasher relay. On many newer cars the turn signals are run by the body control module — then a scan tool diagnosis is needed.

One side stays on and the hazards don’t change it, or the signal flashes once and goes out — check the alarm. Its module is usually under the dash in the driver’s footwell. Unplug its connectors: if the turn signal works normally, the problem is the alarm or how it was wired in.
If an alarm was removed earlier, look for leftover wires: over bumps they touch the body and short the turn signal circuit to ground.
Trailer turn signals don’t flash — check the trailer socket and its contacts: corrosion is a common cause.
Truck: trailer turn signals don’t flash — check the trailer socket and its contacts: corrosion is a common cause.
Instrument lights off: check the dimmer

Most often the illumination has simply been turned all the way down with the dimmer — a thumbwheel or buttons on the dash, or a setting in the instrument cluster menu. The instrument lights are also usually powered together with the parking lights: if the parking lights are off too, their fuse is to blame.
A Mitsubishi Pajero 2007 came in with the instrument lights off. The dimmer was in the wrong position — we turned it up and the lights came on. No bulbs or cluster repair were needed.
Turn on the parking lights or low beams and turn the dimmer all the way up. It can be a thumbwheel left of the steering wheel, buttons on the cluster or an item in the menu.
On many cars with automatic headlights the illumination is deliberately dimmed in daylight. Check in the dark or with the light sensor on the dash covered.
Parking lights are off too — check the parking light fuse (below): the instrument and switch illumination is often on the same fuse.
Parking lights work, the dimmer is at maximum, but there’s no illumination — the dimmer, the cluster connector or the cluster itself needs checking.
If the idle went high or started hunting right after cleaning the throttle body, run a throttle adaptation and idle relearn with a scan tool: the ECU remembers the corrections for the dirty throttle.

Stage 1: the DEF light is on — low level. Stage 2: DEF + Check Engine — even lower level, wrong DEF or SCR fault, slight power loss. Stage 3: DEF almost empty, wrong DEF or an SCR fault lasting over 5 hours — the DEF light flashes, major power loss. Stage 4: + red Stop Engine after refuelling without adding DEF, an hour of idling or a stop — speed limited to 5 mph (~8 km/h); since 2026 Cummins has been releasing US software updates with a final stage of 25 mph. What to do: fill DEF to ISO 22241; if the lights stay on, go to Oleg straight away.
