Daytime running lights (DRL) not working

Most often the culprit is a fuse, the DRL relay, a corroded connector or a burned-out LED module. On newer cars the lights are controlled by the body control module, so the cause can be a fault in it or on the CAN bus, especially after a repair or an accident.
Oleg will check the power, ground, relay and lighting control module, read the fault codes with a scan tool and find where the signal is lost. Mobile service available.
DRLs not working
Daytime running lights not working

First make sure the lights are supposed to be on: on most cars the DRLs only come on with the engine running and go out or dim when the parking lights or low beams are on. In automatic mode, the low beams replace them in the dark.
If one side is out, check the module itself and its connector: corrosion, moisture, a loose plug. If the DRLs use bulbs, swap the left and right bulbs. An LED module is usually replaced as a unit.

If both sides are out, check the DRL fuse (labeled DRL on the fuse box lid; on some cars the lights are fed from the headlight or parking light fuses) and the DRL relay: swap it with a nearby relay that has the same marking.

With the engine running, measure the voltage at the DRL connector with a multimeter: it should be about the same as at the battery, 13.5–14.5 V. Voltage present but the light is off — the ground or the module itself. No voltage — look for an open circuit, the relay or the control module.

If the DRLs were added aftermarket rather than factory-fitted, many such modules only switch the lights on when system voltage is above about 13 V, that is, when the alternator is charging. Measure at the battery terminals with the engine running: below 13.5 V — check the alternator.

If the DRLs flicker, switch off by themselves, only work with the low beams on, or a lighting fault shows on the dash, a scan-tool diagnosis is needed: the body control module stores bulb and CAN bus fault codes.
High beams not working

If one side is out, it is almost always the bulb or its socket. Out on both sides — a fuse, relay, the stalk switch or the ground. On newer cars the high beams are controlled by the body control module, and then the fault codes are read with a scan tool.
If the headlights are xenon, don’t take them apart yourself: the ballast produces high voltage.
Don’t replace parts at random. I usually find the cause in 10–20 minutes by going in order: bulb, fuse, relay, power at the headlight, ground.
Oleg will check the bulbs, fuses, relay, power and ground at the headlight, and on newer cars read the body control module codes. Mobile service available.

If the high beam is out in one headlight, remove the bulb (on H4 the low and high beams are in one bulb, on two filaments). A broken filament or darkened glass means it has burned out. To check, swap the bulbs. A darkened or melted socket is overheating — replace it.

If the high beams are out on both sides, check the high-beam fuses (HEAD HI, H-LP HI, sometimes one per headlight, see below) and the relay: it clicks when you switch on the high beams. No click — swap the relay with a nearby one that has the same marking.

If the fuse blows again, there is a short in the circuit. Don’t fit a higher rating: look for a chafed wire or a melted headlight connector. If you smell burning near the fuse box, don’t use the lights until it’s repaired.

Pull the stalk toward you to flash the high beams. If flashing works but the high beams won’t stay on in the locked position, or you have to “find” the right stalk position, the stalk switch is often to blame: clean the contacts or replace it.

With the high beams on, measure the voltage across the headlight connector terminals: about 12 V, nearly the same as at the battery. 12 V between positive and the body but less across the terminals means a bad ground. No positive — look for an open circuit back to the relay.

If the light is dim, flickers or cuts out when you wiggle the wires, or the headlight connector gets hot, there is a bad contact: clean the connector and the ground. Use bulbs of the wattage the headlight is designed for: higher-wattage and cheap bulbs overheat the socket.

A lighting warning on the dash, one side not working and no response to the switch — on VW, Audi, Skoda, BMW and Mercedes the body control module (BCM) or the CAN bus is often to blame. A scan-tool diagnosis is needed.
In a 24 V system only fit 24 V bulbs — a 12 V bulb will blow immediately.
Truck: in a 24 V system only fit 24 V bulbs — a 12 V bulb will blow immediately.
License plate light not working

The license plate light comes on with the parking lights and is usually on the same fuse. Most often the bulb has burned out or the contacts in the light housing have corroded; less often a wire has broken near the trunk lid. You can be fined for an unlit plate.
Oleg will find the break or the corroded contact and repair the wiring in the trunk lid boot. Mobile service available.
License plate light not working
Turn on the parking lights. If the tail lights are out too, check the TAIL parking light fuse (below): the plate light is on it as well.

If the tail lights work but the plate light doesn’t, remove the light housing (clips or two screws) and take out the bulb, usually a W5W. A broken filament or darkened glass — replace it. Test with a bulb you know is good.
Inspect the contacts in the housing: green deposits, rust or water — clean them; the bulb must sit snugly. If there is moisture inside, replace the housing or its seal, or it will happen again.
With the parking lights on, measure the voltage at the housing connector: about 12 V. If it’s there, the bulb or the housing is at fault. If not, look for an open circuit in the wiring.
The wire most often breaks in the rubber boot between the body and the trunk lid (liftgate). Turn on the parking lights and flex the boot: if the light flickers, the break is there.
If an LED bulb you fitted doesn’t light, turn it 180°: LEDs have polarity. On cars where the body control module monitors the bulbs, you need a bulb marked CANbus.
If the trailer plate light is out, check the trailer socket and its contacts: corrosion is a common cause.
Truck: if the trailer plate light is out, check the trailer socket and its contacts: corrosion is a common cause.
Fog lights: why they don’t work and how to wire them

If one fog light is out, it’s almost always the bulb. If both are out — the fuse, relay, switch, power or ground. If you’re installing fog lights yourself, wire them only through a relay and a separate fuse.
Never wire fog lights straight through the switch without a relay and fuse: the switch and wires overheat and melt, and a short can set the wiring on fire.
When both fog lights are out at once, I look for the cause in the fuse, relay or power supply — bulbs rarely burn out together. And very often it’s a bad ground.
Oleg will wire your fog lights the right way — through a relay and fuse — or find out why the factory ones don’t work. Mobile service available.
Fog lights: repair and wiring
Fog lights not working

First turn on the parking lights or low beams: on many cars the fog lights won’t come on without them. If one is out, swap the left and right bulbs. If the fault moves with the bulb, replace the bulbs, preferably both at once.

If both are out, check the FOG fuse and the fog light relay. The relay should click when you press the switch. No click — swap the relay with a nearby one that has the same marking, or check the switch.

With the fog lights on, measure at the light’s connector: about 12 V across the terminals. 12 V between positive and the body but less across the terminals means a bad ground. No positive at all — the relay, switch or an open circuit.
If they work intermittently or flicker, the connectors have corroded: fog lights sit low, in dirt and water. Unplug them, clean the contacts and protect them from moisture.
Wiring through a 4-pin relay: 30 — battery positive through the fuse, 87 — output to both lights (wired in parallel), 85 — ground, 86 — the wire from the switch.

Put the fuse in the positive wire as close to the battery as possible. Two 55 W halogen fog lights draw about 9 A, so 15 A is enough. The rating must not exceed what the wire can carry: no more than 15 A for 1.5 mm² wire.

The power wire to the lights should be copper, at least 1.5 mm², better 2.5 mm²; 4 mm² for high-power LED lights. Feed the switch from the parking light circuit or the ignition: it only carries the small current to 86, and the fog lights can’t be left on to drain the battery.

Attach the lights’ ground and relay pin 85 to clean bare body metal. Mount the relay in a dry spot under the hood; make connections with crimps and heat shrink, no twisted splices. Run the wires in a protective loom.
Turn signal flashing fast or hazards not working

If the turn signals work but the hazards don’t, the hazard switch or its HAZ fuse is to blame (it can be separate from TURN, see below). Press the switch several times: if it works only sometimes or only when pressed hard, the contacts are worn — the switch is repaired or replaced.

If you switch on the hazards and all the turn signals stay lit without flashing, with no clicking, the flasher relay has failed: it’s shared by the turn signals and the hazards. Replace it with a good one of the same type.

If all the bulbs are good but the turn signal flashes fast, dimly or intermittently, check the socket contacts (green deposits, burn marks) and the tail light ground. A sign of a bad ground is the brake or parking light flickering along with the turn signal.
How to check the brake lights

You can check the brake lights on your own: back up to a wall or gate, switch on the ignition, press the brake and look at the reflection in the mirror. Or ask someone to stand behind the car. There are usually three — left, right and the high-mounted one.

If one brake light is out, the bulb has blown. Open the trunk, remove the tail light assembly and take out the bulb (P21W or the dual-filament P21/5W): if the filament is broken, replace it. If a new one doesn’t light either, look for corrosion in the socket.

Check the brake light switch with a multimeter: one of its wires has 12 V with the ignition on (on many cars, all the time), and the other should only get 12 V when the pedal is pressed. Power on the input but none on the output — replace the switch.
Backup camera not working
Most often it’s a lost connection: a chafed wire, a corroded connector, or no power from the reverse light circuit. Less often, moisture inside the camera or the head unit’s video input is to blame.
In my experience, about 80% of the time a camera fails for simple reasons: wiring, power or moisture. That’s where I start.
Oleg will check the power, ground, video cable and head unit input, and the CAN bus on cars with factory infotainment. Mobile service available.

Switch on the ignition, select reverse and see whether the reverse lights come on. The camera is often powered from them: if they don’t light, check the bulb, the fuse and the reverse light switch on the transmission.
Wipe the lens. In winter the camera can freeze, and after a car wash it can fog up inside: let it dry out somewhere warm.

With reverse selected, measure the voltage at the camera connector: about 12 V between positive and ground. None — look for a break from the reverse light circuit. It’s there but the screen is black — the camera or the video cable to the head unit.
If it works intermittently or the picture has interference, inspect the rear connectors and the wire in the rubber boot between the body and the trunk lid: wires often break and corrode there.

A blue screen or “no signal” — check in the head unit settings that the camera input is enabled. If the camera has power but there’s no picture, the camera (moisture, burned-out sensor) or the head unit’s video input is faulty.

If it never worked after installation, flickers or comes on with a delay, check the polarity, the camera ground and the reverse trigger wire to the head unit: that signal is what switches the head unit to the camera.
Wiper not working or not wiping well
A rear wiper most often fails because of the fuse, a broken wire in the trunk lid boot, the motor or a seized shaft. Poor wiping is usually down to worn or dirty blades.

If on a car with a liftgate the rear wiper, plate light, rear defroster or camera all stop working at once, the first thing I check is the wiring in the boot between the body and the liftgate — that’s where it breaks most often.
Oleg will find the break in the boot and check the switch, motor and wiper linkage. Mobile service available.
Wipers not working
Check the wiper fuse — labeled WIPER, RR WIPER or RR WIP on the fuse box lid. In winter, first check whether the blade is frozen to the glass: don’t switch on frozen wipers, warm up the glass first.

Switch on the rear wiper and listen at the trunk lid. Motor hums but the blade doesn’t move — the shaft has seized or the arm splines are stripped. Motor is silent — no power, a faulty switch or the motor itself.
With the wiper switched on, measure the voltage at the motor connector: about 12 V. If it’s there but the motor doesn’t turn, replace the motor. If not, check the stalk switch and the wiring.
Inspect the wires in the boot between the body and the trunk lid: with the wiper on, slowly open and close the lid. If the wiper jerks or stops, a wire has broken inside the boot.

If it leaves streaks and smears, the rubber has lost its flexibility, cracked or worn down. Replace the blades every 6–12 months and choose ones made for your car and the season: cheap universal blades wear out faster.

Before replacing the blades, wash the glass and wipe the rubber with a soapy sponge: tree sap, tar and poplar fluff cause squeaking and missed spots. If the blade doesn’t press well at the edges, the arm spring has weakened or the blade is at the wrong angle.
If the wipers move in jerks, slowly, or stop mid-glass, the motor, gearbox or linkage is worn. The wiper drive needs repair.
Where the washer reservoir is and where to add fluid

The washer reservoir is almost always under the hood, near a fender or headlight. Usually one reservoir serves both the windshield and the rear window: fluid reaches the rear nozzle through a hose running the length of the car.
When a washer doesn’t work, I check the fluid level, the pump motor on the reservoir, the connectors and the power. Very often it’s something simple: an empty reservoir or corroded contacts.
Oleg will check the washer pump, its connector and power supply, and find any break in the wiring. Mobile service available.
Where is the washer reservoir
Washer reservoir, washer not working
Open the hood and look for a white or translucent plastic reservoir with a blue, yellow or black cap. The cap shows a windshield symbol with water spray. It opens without tools.
Don’t confuse it with the coolant expansion tank or the brake fluid reservoir: only the washer has the windshield-and-spray symbol.

If you can’t see it, it may be under the front bumper, below the cowl at the base of the windshield, behind a fender liner or in the headlight recess. Then only the filler neck with the same cap is visible under the hood.
On older vehicles the rear window may have its own reservoir inside the rear door — for example, on the Toyota Prado 90 and 95 series.

If the rear washer doesn’t spray, check the fluid level, and in winter whether it has frozen: use winter washer fluid, not water. Clear the nozzle with a thin needle and check that the hose hasn’t come off.

Operate the washer and listen for the pump on the reservoir. If it’s silent, check its connector for corrosion and the voltage there with the stalk held: about 12 V. If there’s voltage but the pump stays silent, replace the pump.
Instrument cluster not working

The cluster has gone completely dead or works intermittently. Most often it’s a fuse, a corroded connector or ground, or no power. Less often it’s the cluster itself (circuit board, gauge motors) or the CAN bus.
Without the cluster you can’t see your speed, engine temperature, or the oil pressure and charging warning lights. Don’t drive far until it’s fixed.
Oleg will check the cluster’s power, ground and CAN bus, read the fault codes with a scan tool and find whether the cause is in the wiring or the cluster itself. Mobile service available.

Check the battery: about 12.6 V with the engine off. If the glitches began after the battery went flat or after a jump start, charge it, switch off the ignition and disconnect the negative terminal for a few minutes: the modules will reset.

Check the cluster fuses — labeled METER, GAUGE, CLUSTER or DOME on the fuse box lid. The cluster usually has two feeds: constant and ignition-switched. If a fuse blows again there’s a short — don’t fit a higher rating.

Inspect the cluster connectors, the plugs under the dash and the body ground: corrosion, moisture, a loose plug. Sometimes reseating a connector is enough. Before removing the cluster, disconnect the negative terminal and don’t touch the yellow airbag connectors.

Using the car’s wiring diagram, measure at the cluster connector: 12 V on the constant feed at all times, and on the ignition feed with the ignition on. With the cluster plugged in, there should be no more than 0.2 V between its ground and battery negative.
Check for water under the dash and on the driver’s side floor: water leaking from under the windshield often floods connectors.

If the cluster glitches, the needles behave erratically, readings drop out or fault messages appear, a scan-tool diagnosis is needed: the CAN bus or the cluster itself (circuit board, chips, gauge motors) is to blame. The cluster is repaired or replaced.
On a 24 V system there should be about 24 V at the cluster connector.
Truck: on a 24 V system there should be about 24 V at the cluster connector.
Where the fuse box is
There are usually two: inside the cabin under the dashboard on the driver’s side, and under the hood next to the battery. Many European and premium cars have a third one in the trunk.
Don’t fit a fuse with a higher rating and don’t bridge it with wire: the wiring can melt and catch fire.

Sometimes what looks like a serious breakdown is one small fuse: the lights, radio, power windows or heater stop working, or the car won’t start. If the fuse blows again, that means a short or a faulty device, and it has to be tracked down.
Oleg will find the fuse boxes and the right fuse on your car, and if it keeps blowing, he’ll find the short in the circuit. Mobile service available.
Where’s the fuse box
Finding the fuse box

Cabin: look under the steering column by the driver’s knees, on the end of the dashboard on the driver’s side (visible with the door open), left or right of the instrument cluster, and in or behind the glovebox. The box has a plastic cover held by clips.
Under the hood: look for a box with a lid next to the battery, by the fender or near the engine control module. This one holds the high-current fuses and the relays.
Trunk: an extra box may sit behind a side trim panel or next to the battery if it’s mounted at the rear. This is common on European and premium cars.
Can’t find it? Look for a cover marked FUSE or with a lightning bolt symbol, and check the owner’s manual. The power distribution box is almost always next to the battery.
The labeled diagram is on the inside of the lid or in the owner’s manual. Take a photo of it with your phone, and keep a fuse puller and spare fuses of your type in the glovebox.

Once you’ve found the box, inspect the fuse in question and its contacts: the link inside is intact, with no corrosion or signs of melting. Replace it only with the same rating — it will be the same color.
Many trucks run on 24 V. Only fit a fuse of the same rating and check the diagram on the fuse box lid.
Truck: many trucks run on 24 V. Only fit a fuse of the same rating and check the diagram on the fuse box lid.
How to check fuses yourself

A fuse blows on an overload or a short, protecting the wiring and control modules — it’s the result, not the cause. You can check it by eye, with a test light or with a multimeter. If it blows again or melts, look for the cause in the circuit.
Never fit a higher-rated fuse, even “temporarily”, and never bridge it with wire: the wiring will melt, the ECU may fail or the car may catch fire.

Before replacing expensive parts, start with the fuses. And don’t buy the cheapest no-name fuses: the body says 15 A, but it actually carries much more — instead of blowing in time, it melts together with the holder and overheats the wiring.
Oleg will find out why the fuse keeps blowing or melting — a short, an overload or a poor contact — and repair the circuit or the fuse box. Mobile service available.
How to check fuses
Checking fuses

Turn off the ignition. Find the fuse using the diagram on the fuse box lid, pull it out with the fuse puller and hold it up to the light: if the link inside is broken or darkened, it’s blown. A mini fuse can look fine, so testing with a meter is more reliable.

With a test light, without removing the fuse: clip one lead to ground (bare metal on the body or engine) and touch the probe to each of the two metal test points on top of the fuse in turn. Check ignition-fed circuits with the ignition on; constant-power circuits (hazard lights, alarm) can be checked with it off.

The light is equally bright on both sides — the fuse is good. Only on one side — it’s blown. On neither side — no power is reaching it, keep looking upstream. Noticeably different brightness — a poor contact or corrosion in the fuse box. Always check both test points.

With a multimeter: pull the fuse, set continuity mode or resistance on the 200 Ω range, and put the probes on both blades. A beep or about 0 Ω — it’s good; “1” or OL on the display — it’s blown. Without removing it, in DC voltage mode: there should be about 12 V on both sides.

Replace it only with the same rating — it will be the same color. If a new one blows right away, there’s a short in the circuit or a faulty load: inspect the wiring and connectors for corrosion, and check the relay and the pump, motor or module itself.

If the fuse or its holder gets hot, smells of burnt plastic or the body has melted, the cause is a poor contact, an overload or a poor-quality fuse. Inspect the socket: if it’s darkened or melted, it needs repair — just fitting a new fuse isn’t enough.
Wire add-on equipment — LED headlights, audio, amplifiers, inverters, a parking heater — through a relay and its own fuse. Without a relay the circuit is overloaded and heats up.
A relay is chattering or clicking rapidly

A healthy relay clicks once when it switches on. Chattering or rapid clicking means its contacts keep closing and opening. Most often the relay isn’t getting enough voltage: a weak battery or a poor contact at the terminals or ground. Less often the relay itself is worn or the wiring is damaged.
Most often a relay chatters not because it’s broken but because it isn’t getting enough voltage. So start with the battery, terminals and ground, and replace the relay only after that.
Oleg will check the power, ground and relay circuit under load and find where the voltage is lost. Mobile service available.
Relay is chattering
Relay chattering

Note when it chatters: when you switch on the ignition, when starting, when the fan or the alarm is working. Rhythmic clicking with the turn signals or hazard lights on is normal — that’s how the flasher relay works.

Measure the battery voltage with a multimeter in DC voltage mode. Engine off — 12.4–12.9 V; while cranking — no lower than 9.6–10 V. Lower than that — charge or replace the battery: chattering when starting, a dash that goes dark and a clicking starter usually come from this.

Check the battery terminals: they don’t wobble and have no white or green deposits. Check the ground: the cable from the negative to the body and from the engine to the body, bolts tight, no corrosion.
Find the chattering relay by ear or by touching its case with a finger. Inspect its socket and the fuse for that circuit: corrosion, darkening, melted plastic.
Swap the relay with a neighboring one that has the same marking on its case. If the chattering moves with the relay, its contacts are burnt and bouncing — replace the relay.
If it’s the starter solenoid chattering and the battery and terminals are fine, the cause is in the starter: the solenoid, the brushes or the starter wiring.

Power, ground and the relay are fine, but the chattering remains — look in the wiring: damaged wires, connectors not fully latched, a short. This often happens after a repair. Message Oleg — he’ll tell you what to do next.
For a 24 V system: engine off — about 25 V; while cranking, healthy batteries drop to 20–22 V. Also check the link cable between the batteries.
Truck: for a 24 V system: engine off — about 25 V; while cranking, healthy batteries drop to 20–22 V. Also check the link cable between the batteries.
How to check the ground

Ground is the connection of the battery negative to the body and the engine: current returns to the battery through it. A bad ground causes slow cranking, dim or flickering headlights, a misbehaving instrument cluster and electronic fault codes.
Connect the test wire only to the battery negative. If it touches the positive and the body at the same time, you’ll get a short circuit with sparks and burns.

Many electrical faults aren’t the battery or the alternator but a bad ground. It most often fails on the body next to the battery, on the engine, on the transmission and where the wiring is bolted to the body — start with those spots.
Oleg will measure the voltage drop on every ground under load, find the poor connection and restore it. Mobile service available.
Checking the ground

Inspect the ground cables: from the battery negative to the body, from the engine to the body, and on the transmission. The bolts are tight, there’s no corrosion, dirt or rust on or under the lugs, and the cable isn’t broken.

Simple test: press one end of a heavy wire to the negative battery terminal and the other to bare metal on the engine. Try to start the car. If the starter cranks faster and the car starts normally, the ground is bad.

With a multimeter: DC voltage mode, 20 V range. Black probe on the battery’s negative post (on the post itself, not the terminal clamp), red probe on bare metal on the engine or on the starter housing.

Have a helper crank the engine and watch the meter. Normal is up to 0.2–0.3 V. More than that — a poor ground connection. With no load, the meter reads almost 0 even with a bad ground, so measure only while cranking.
Check the body ground the same way: red probe on the body next to the battery, with the headlights and the blower on high. The spec is the same — no more than 0.2–0.3 V.

Found a bad ground? Remove the bolt, clean the metal and the lug down to bare shine, coat the joint with protective contact grease and tighten it well. If the cable is corroded inside or broken, replace it.
After the repair, measure again while cranking. If the drop is still there, the problem is further along in the wiring or the modules. Message Oleg — he’ll tell you what to do next.
On a truck, the ground goes through the battery disconnect switch to the frame: check its contacts and the cable to the frame the same way — by measuring while cranking.
Truck: on a truck, the ground goes through the battery disconnect switch to the frame: check its contacts and the cable to the frame the same way — by measuring while cranking.
How to check the starter yourself

Before replacing the starter, make sure it’s really at fault: a click with no cranking, slow cranking or silence can also come from a weak battery, the terminals, the ground or the control circuit. Check in order: battery, starter power feed, control signal, then the starter itself.

Never run the starter by bridging its terminals with a screwdriver: that bypasses the interlocks, and a car in gear will drive off. Crank for no more than 10 seconds at a time, with 30–60 second pauses. Keep your hands and the test leads away from the belts and the fan.

Don’t rush to replace the starter: often the start fails because of a relay, the ignition switch, an alarm or the immobilizer. Battery and terminals first, then the starter power feed, then the starter itself — that way you won’t buy a part you don’t need.
Oleg will test the starter and the starting circuit right on the car, find where the current is lost and, if needed, remove the starter for repair. Mobile service available.
How to check the starter
Checking the starter
Prepare the car: automatic in P, manual in neutral, parking brake on. You need a helper at the wheel and a multimeter in DC voltage mode on the 20 V range.
Check the battery: 12.4–12.9 V with the engine off. If it’s lower, charge it first — testing a starter on a discharged battery is pointless. The terminals are tight and free of deposits.
Have the helper crank the engine while you measure the voltage at the battery posts: no lower than 9.6–10 V. If it drops below that, the battery is weak or the terminals are bad.

Positive cable: red probe on the battery’s positive post, black probe on the starter’s heavy terminal (30), while cranking. Normal is up to 0.5 V. More than that — a poor connection or a damaged cable.
Ground: red probe on the starter housing, black probe on the battery’s negative post, while cranking. Normal is up to 0.2–0.3 V.

Control signal: black probe to ground, red probe on the solenoid’s thin wire (terminal 50). With the key in START, it should read almost the same as the battery. No voltage — the starter isn’t to blame: check the starter fuse and relay, the selector or clutch interlock, and the ignition switch.

If there’s voltage at terminal 50 but the starter only clicks, the starter itself is faulty: solenoid, brushes, contacts. If it whirs but doesn’t turn the engine — the Bendix drive. If it cranks slowly with normal readings — a worn starter or an engine that’s hard to turn.
For a 24 V system: the battery pair reads 24.8–25.8 V at rest, and healthy batteries drop to 20–22 V while cranking. Check the battery disconnect switch and the link cable between the batteries.

Truck: for a 24 V system: the battery pair reads 24.8–25.8 V at rest, and healthy batteries drop to 20–22 V while cranking. Check the battery disconnect switch and the link cable between the batteries.

Don’t just recharge the battery: if it went flat overnight, there’s a reason, and it won’t go away. From experience: a faulty audio amplifier drew 0.2 A and drained the battery overnight, an alarm with corroded wires drained it in 2–3 days, and an old power window module drew 0.1 A while switched off.
Find a parasitic draw
Finding a parasitic draw

Measure the parasitic draw. Turn off the ignition and everything else, and close the doors. Remove the negative terminal. Set the multimeter to DC amps with the red lead in the 10 A jack. Connect the meter between the battery’s negative post and the removed terminal.

Wait for the modules to go to sleep — anywhere from a few minutes to an hour; don’t open the doors during this time. Normal is about 20–70 mA (0.02–0.07 A). Noticeably more, say 0.1–0.2 A, means there’s a draw.

Without disconnecting the meter, pull the fuses one at a time. The one that makes the current drop sharply is on the circuit with the draw: check everything it powers. While the meter is connected, don’t turn on the ignition or start the engine — it will burn out the multimeter.
Battery terminal gets hot

A hot terminal always means resistance in the circuit: a poor contact, corrosion, a worn-out clamp or a damaged cable. It causes voltage drop and hard starting, and the clamp or cable can melt and catch fire.

If the clamp or cable has melted or you smell burning, don’t start the car — disconnect the negative terminal and message Oleg. Don’t overtighten the clamps: you can break the clamp or the battery post.

A hot terminal means there’s resistance in the circuit, and that means voltage drop and a fire risk. Don’t put it off. Very often the culprit isn’t the clamp itself but the ground: a poor body-to-engine connection or corroded mounting points.
Oleg will measure the voltage drop across the terminals, cables and ground under load, find where the resistance is and replace the clamp or cable. Mobile service available.
Hot battery terminal

After a drive, switch off the engine and carefully feel what’s warm: just the clamp, the cable lug, or the cable along its length. If the heat runs along the cable, the problem is inside the cable or in its crimp.
Remove the clamps: negative first, then positive. Clean the clamps and battery posts down to bare metal with sandpaper or a wire brush, removing all white or green deposits.
Inspect the clamp: if it’s cracked, stretched, or still turns on the post with the bolt fully tightened, replace it. Soft, cheap clamps deform quickly and start heating up again.

Inspect the cable next to the clamp: the insulation is intact, with no swelling or green corrosion under it, and the lug is crimped tight. Corroded strands and a poor crimp get hot — replace the lug or the cable.
Refit the clamps: positive first, then negative. Tighten them so the clamp can’t be turned by hand, but without excess force.
Check the ground: the cable from the negative to the body and the engine-to-body strap, with their bolts and lugs. A bad ground makes the terminal heat up under the starter’s load.

Check with a multimeter in DC voltage mode: one probe on the battery post, the other on the clamp itself, while a helper cranks the engine. Normal is no more than 0.1 V across the connection. More than that — the contact is poor and the terminal will heat up.
Car gives electric shocks

A small jolt in your finger, a snap or a spark when you get out and touch the door is static electricity: the body and your clothing build up a charge while driving. It’s harmless and not a sign of a fault. If it shocks you with the engine running or during repairs, check the ground and the wiring.
On a hybrid or an EV, a shock from the body can be a sign of high-voltage leakage. Don’t touch the orange cables, don’t drive the car, and message Oleg.

If it only shocks you when you get out, especially in winter, that’s static and needs no repair: hold the door pillar as you get out. A healthy battery won’t shock you through the body. If the shocks are strong or there are other electrical faults, I check the ground, the parasitic draw and the wiring.
Oleg will check the grounds, measure the parasitic draw, and test the alternator and the wiring of any add-on equipment. Mobile service available.
Electric shocks from the car
Note when it happens. Only when getting out, at the moment you touch the door or the body, more often in winter and in synthetic clothing — that’s static.
To avoid it: before you stand up from the seat, grab the metal door pillar and hold on until you’re out. The charge drains away without a jolt.
Remove synthetic seat covers, treat the interior with antistatic spray and keep the air humidity normal. Antistatic grounding straps don’t always help.

If touching the body shocks you with the engine running or during repairs, it’s no longer static. Check the ground: the cables from the battery negative to the body and from the engine to the body, with their bolts and lugs — tight and free of corrosion.
Think about what has been added: an alarm, an audio system, extra lights, a parking heater. Damaged insulation on their wiring is a common source. Don’t touch bare wires with your hands.

If the shocks are strong and constant, and there are also starting problems, flickering lights or a battery that drains quickly, message Oleg: it needs a parasitic draw test and checks of the grounds, alternator and wiring.
How to replace the alarm key fob battery
If the car only responds up close, ignores commands or the LED on the fob barely lights up, the battery has most likely run down. Replacing it takes a few minutes.
Keep coin batteries away from children: swallowing one is life-threatening. If you suspect a child has swallowed one, see a doctor immediately.
If the car only responds to the fob up close and the LED is dim, it’s almost always the battery, not the alarm. Start there.
Oleg will check the fob and the alarm unit and, if the fob has lost its pairing, re-pair it to your alarm — with the vehicle documents. Mobile service available.
Key fob battery
Key fob battery
Find out the battery type: most often CR2032, CR2025 or CR2016, less often AAA or AA. The type is printed on the battery itself or inside the fob. Buy the same one.
Open the case with a small screwdriver, a coin or by the latch. Insert the tool into the slot at the seam between the halves and twist gently so you don’t break the plastic.
Before removing the old battery, note which way it sits — where the plus (+) and minus are. The plus side usually faces up, but taking a photo is safer.
Fit the new battery the same way round. Don’t touch the contacts with dirty or greasy fingers — hold the battery by its edge.
Snap the case shut all the way around and test it: arm and disarm the alarm.

Still not working? Inspect the battery contacts in the fob and gently clean off any corrosion with a pencil eraser. If that doesn’t help, a button or the circuit board is broken, the fob has lost its pairing, or the alarm unit is faulty.
Water in the cabin or under the floor mat

Water under the floor mat is no small thing: it corrodes connectors, damages the modules under the seats and the wiring in the floor, ruins body grounds and can lead to shorts and starting problems. The usual culprits are clogged sunroof, cowl or A/C drains, a windshield after replacement, the doors or a leak at the rear.
Airbag connectors run under the seats and in the floor — they’re yellow. Don’t unplug or touch them, even while you’re drying the cabin.

Just drying the mats isn’t enough: if you don’t find where the water comes from, it will come back. And if you put it off, instead of clearing a drain you’ll be repairing modules and wiring and paying for complex diagnostics.
Oleg will check the connectors, modules and grounds after water exposure, find the corroded contacts and restore the wiring. Mobile service available.
Water in the cabin

Take out the floor mats and feel the carpet, especially underneath: moisture can build up under it unnoticed for a long time. Note where it’s wet: on the driver’s side, the front passenger side or at the rear.

Wet on the front passenger side — check the cowl under the windshield: if the drain holes are clogged with leaves, the water rises and gets into the cabin through the heater air intake. A clogged A/C drain leaks the same way.

If you have a sunroof or a panoramic roof, clear its drain tubes: when they’re clogged, water runs down the pillars behind the trim and under the carpet. If the windshield was replaced, water may run down the pillars behind the dashboard, toward the fuse box.

Check the doors: the drain holes at the bottom of the door are clear, the plastic vapor barrier behind the door panel is intact, and the weatherstrips aren’t torn. Water inside the door is normal, but it has to drain out.
Wet at the rear or across the whole floor — check the trunk lid seal, the tail lights and the body vent flaps: water from there runs forward under the carpet.

Fix the source, then dry the cabin completely — including the carpet and what’s underneath it, not just the surface. Otherwise the damp smell and window fogging will stay, and the connectors will keep corroding.

Inspect the connectors and modules under the seats and in the floor, and the ground points on the floor: green deposits, water in the connectors. If electrical glitches or starting problems appear, message Oleg — he’ll tell you what to do next.
How to test the camshaft position sensor

The camshaft position sensor (CMP) tells the ECU where the camshaft is, so it can time fuel injection and spark precisely. Signs of a fault: long cranking before the engine starts or no start at all, unstable rpm, loss of power, higher fuel consumption, stalling while driving, Check Engine light on.
Before replacing the sensor, I always check the power supply, wiring and connectors. People very often replace the sensor and the problem stays — because it was the wiring or the ECU all along.
Oleg will check the sensor signal with a scan tool and an oscilloscope, the wiring and the timing mark alignment. Mobile service available.
Test camshaft sensor
Camshaft sensor check

Read the codes with a scan tool: P0340 — camshaft position sensor circuit, P0341 — signal out of range. P0016–P0019 mean crank/cam correlation: most often a stretched timing chain or a timing belt that has jumped a tooth, not the sensor.

Find the sensor: it is usually on the cylinder head next to the camshaft, sometimes near the timing belt or chain. Inspect the connector and wires: is the plug fully seated, any corrosion on the pins, broken or chafed wires? A poor contact is very often the culprit.

Check the power supply: unplug the connector, turn the ignition on and measure with a multimeter between the power wire and ground — you should see 5 V or 12 V, depending on the car. No power means an open in the wiring or an ECU problem: don’t replace the sensor yet.

Check the signal: with the sensor plugged in, back-probe the signal wire with a thin probe and measure it against ground while a helper cranks the engine. The voltage should jump between 0 and the supply voltage; if it doesn’t move, there is no signal. An oscilloscope will show clean square-wave pulses.
In the scan tool live data, rpm should appear while cranking. Some cars also show a cam/crank sync parameter: if there is rpm but no sync, check the camshaft sensor and the timing marks.

Start test: with the ignition off, unplug the sensor and try to start the engine. If it starts better, the sensor is probably sending a bad signal, and without it the ECU has switched to backup mode. Then plug it back in and clear the code.

Don’t confuse it with the crankshaft sensor: the symptoms are similar. With no crank signal the engine usually won’t start at all and the tachometer stays at zero while cranking. With no cam signal the engine usually still starts, but cranks longer.
How to test the crankshaft position sensor

The crankshaft position sensor (CKP) tells the ECU the engine rpm and crankshaft position — the ECU uses it to fire the spark and the injectors. With no signal, the engine cranks but won’t start, or stalls while driving. Other signs: unstable rpm, Check Engine light on, the tachometer reading dropping out.
Don’t drive with a faulty crankshaft sensor: the engine can stall at any moment, including while driving, and may not restart.
Very often the problem isn’t the sensor itself but corroded contacts, damaged wiring or a poor ground. So I don’t rush to replace the sensor — first I check everything step by step.
Oleg will check the crankshaft sensor signal with a scan tool and an oscilloscope, plus the wiring and ground — including on a hot engine. Mobile service available.
Test crankshaft sensor
Crankshaft sensor check

Crank the engine and watch the tachometer and the rpm in the scan tool live data: while cranking you normally see about 150–300 rpm. If it stays at zero, the ECU isn’t getting a crank signal. Sensor codes: P0335 — circuit, P0336 — signal out of range.

Find the sensor: it is usually near the crankshaft pulley, on the engine block, or by the flywheel on the transmission side. Inspect the connector (corrosion) and wires (breaks, chafing). Remove the sensor and clean the tip of oil, dirt and metal shavings.

Count the wires at the connector. Two wires (sometimes a third one is the shield) — an inductive sensor: test it by resistance. Three wires (power, ground, signal) — a Hall-effect sensor: resistance tells you nothing, check the power and the signal.

Inductive sensor: unplug it, set the multimeter to ohms and put the probes on the sensor pins. Typically 500–1000 Ω (check the manual for the exact figure). Infinite (open circuit) — the sensor is bad; nearly 0 Ω — a short. Within spec — the sensor is probably OK.

An inductive sensor generates its own signal: with the connector unplugged and the meter on AC volts, it should read at least a few tenths of a volt while cranking. An oscilloscope will show a sine wave with a gap from the missing teeth on the trigger wheel (for example, 60−2).

Hall-effect sensor: with the ignition on, the connector should have a 5 V or 12 V supply and a good ground. While cranking, the signal wire jumps between 0 and the supply voltage; on an oscilloscope it’s a clean square wave with the same gap.

Does the engine stall when hot and refuse to start, but start again once it cools down? Suspect the crankshaft sensor: they often fail when hot. Test right after it quits, while hot: the cranking rpm on the scan tool and the sensor resistance.
How to test the MAF sensor

The MAF (mass air flow) sensor measures how much air goes into the engine, and the ECU meters fuel based on it. Signs of a fault: hesitation on acceleration, higher fuel consumption, unstable rpm, stalling at idle, hard starting, sometimes a Check Engine light. Other faults cause the same symptoms, so test the sensor first.

A very common mistake is replacing the MAF right away. I first check for vacuum leaks after the sensor, the air filter, the contacts, power, ground and wiring — and only then decide whether the MAF needs replacing.
Oleg will compare the MAF readings with the spec for your engine and check for vacuum leaks and wiring faults. Mobile service available.
Test MAF sensor
MAF sensor check

Quick test: shut the engine off, unplug the MAF sensor and start the engine. If it now runs smoother and pulls better, the MAF is probably reading wrong: without it the ECU goes into limp mode and uses average airflow values. Then plug it back in and clear the code.

Multimeter: turn the ignition on without starting the engine and measure the signal wire against ground with the sensor plugged in (back-probe the connector). On many sensors (for example, Bosch units on Lada cars) a good one reads about 1.0 V; the higher it is, the more worn it is, and 1.2–1.3 V means it’s worn out.

Scan tool: at warm idle with everything switched off, airflow is about 1–1.5 g/s per liter of displacement (a 1.6 L engine — 1.6–2.4 g/s). At 2500 rpm with no load it should be 2.5–3.5 times higher. If the scan tool shows kg/h, divide by 3.6. Compare in the “Sensor norms” section.

Look at the fuel trims: if they are above +10 % both at idle and at 2500 rpm, the MAF is probably reading low. Strongly positive at idle but near zero at 2500 rpm points more to a vacuum leak after the sensor.

Before replacing the sensor, rule out things that cause the same symptoms: a vacuum leak after the MAF (intake boot, clamps), a dirty air filter, corroded contacts and damaged wiring. With the ignition on, the connector must have power and ground.

Cleaning sometimes helps: use only a dedicated MAF sensor cleaner and don’t touch the sensing element. Don’t use carb cleaner — it will ruin the sensor. If the sensor is worn out, cleaning won’t help — only replacement will.
How to test the knock sensor

The knock sensor sits on the engine block and “listens” for knock: when it detects it, the ECU retards the ignition timing. If the sensor or its wire is faulty, the ECU keeps the timing retarded just in case — the engine loses power, hesitates on acceleration, uses more fuel, and the Check Engine light comes on. You may also hear a metallic pinging under acceleration — that’s the knock itself.
The tap test is done with the engine running: keep your hands, clothing and meter leads away from the belts and the fan.
Often the problem isn’t the sensor itself but the wiring under the intake manifold. Many people replace the sensor right away and the cause stays — so I check the wire and the connector first.
Oleg will check the knock sensor and its wiring with a scan tool and an oscilloscope, and look at the ignition timing and knock retard. Mobile service available.
Test knock sensor
Knock sensor check
Read the codes: P0325 — knock sensor circuit, P0326 — signal out of range, P0327 and P0328 — low and high input. Knock sensor codes are common on Toyotas.

Find the sensor: it is bolted to the engine block — usually under the intake manifold or between the cylinders, and you often have to remove the manifold to reach it. Inspect the connector and the wire: a common failure is a wire broken right at the connector and insulation cracked by heat.

Scan tool: on a warm engine, ignition timing at idle is usually 0–20°, and at 2500 rpm with no load 25–40°. If the scan tool shows knock retard, it should normally be about 0°. If timing is always low, the ECU is playing it safe: the sensor, the wiring or bad gas.

Tap test: at warm idle, gently tap the block next to the sensor (not the sensor itself) with a small hammer or a wrench. The live data should show timing retard or a spike in the sensor signal. No reaction means the sensor or the wiring is bad.

Multimeter or oscilloscope: unplug the connector and hook the meter to the sensor pins, with the multimeter on AC millivolts. Tap lightly next to the sensor: a good one produces voltage pulses and the reading jumps. An oscilloscope will show a spike for every tap.

Resistance: with the sensor unplugged, measure between the pins and from each pin to the sensor body. Near 0 Ω or a short to the body means the sensor is bad. The spec varies widely by model — from a few kΩ to hundreds of kΩ or more, so check the manual for your engine.

On installation the sensor must sit flat on clean block metal with its whole mounting face — no washers, paint or sealant. Torque it to the manual spec, usually about 20 N·m. Over- or under-tightened, it either “hears” knock poorly or gives false signals.
If pinging and timing retard showed up after a fill-up and the sensor checks out fine, the cause may be poor-quality gas. Fill up with gas of the right octane rating at a station you trust.
Throttle body: testing and relearn

The electronic throttle body lets air into the engine on command from the ECU. If it’s dirty, has a poor connection or is faulty, the idle hunts or runs high, the engine stalls when you stop, it responds sluggishly to the gas pedal, the Check Engine light comes on, and the car may go into limp mode. Most often the cause is dirt, wiring or a poor contact.
Don’t put your fingers in the throttle bore with the ignition on: an electronic throttle can snap shut and pinch them. Clean it only with the ignition off.
I don’t replace the throttle body right away: 70 % of the time the problem is dirt, wiring or a poor contact. And after cleaning I always do a relearn — otherwise the idle hunts and the car stalls.
Oleg will clean the throttle body, check its sensors and actuator with a scan tool and perform the relearn. Mobile service available.
Throttle: test and relearn
Throttle body problem

Self-test: remove the intake boot, turn the ignition on without starting the engine and watch the throttle plate — on an electronic throttle it should move slightly. If it doesn’t move, check the ECU fuses (below), power at the connector, the wiring and the throttle motor.

Look at the throttle plate: carbon, oil and soot around the edge are enough to cause a rough idle. Clean it with a dedicated throttle body cleaner with the ignition off. Don’t force the plate of an electronic throttle open — you can break the drive gears.

Inspect the throttle body connector: any green corrosion, oxidation or moisture on the pins, are the wires intact? Check the battery too: about 12.6 V with the engine off. With low voltage, the electronic throttle and the ECU misbehave.

The throttle position sensor (TPS) runs on a 5 V reference. With the ignition on, a closed throttle usually reads about 0.5 V; open it slowly (on many cars, by pressing the gas pedal) — the voltage should rise smoothly to about 4.5 V with no jumps or dropouts. Glitches mean a bad sensor.

Scan tool: an electronic throttle has two position sensors, and when you press the pedal both signals should change smoothly and in step. P2135 — the two sensor signals disagree (worn unit or connector); P2101, P2111, P2112 — the actuator or a sticking throttle plate.

After cleaning, removing the throttle body or disconnecting the battery, do a relearn. A simple method that doesn’t work on every car: ignition on for 10–30 seconds, off for 10–30 seconds, then start the engine and don’t touch the gas pedal for 5–10 minutes — the ECU relearns the throttle by itself.

If that didn’t help, warm the engine up at idle until the cooling fan comes on without touching the gas, then drive gently for 10–15 minutes. On some cars the relearn can only be done with a scan tool: resetting the old values and running a forced throttle learn.

A relearn only helps if the throttle is clean and working, with no vacuum leaks and no sensor codes. Common mistakes: revving right after starting, relearning a dirty throttle. If the idle still hunts after the relearn, look for the fault: a relearn doesn’t replace a repair.
Gas pedal not working

On modern cars the gas pedal is electronic: there’s no mechanical link to the throttle, sensors in the pedal tell the ECU how far you’ve pressed it, and the ECU opens the throttle. If the signal is lost or “doesn’t add up”, the car doesn’t respond to the gas or accelerates with a delay, the revs won’t rise, the Check Engine light comes on — the ECU goes into limp mode.

If the car stops responding to the gas pedal completely while driving, turn on the hazard lights, pull over to the shoulder and stop. If it still drives but responds poorly, you can drive on carefully, but don’t put off the check.

I don’t replace parts by guesswork: first the scan tool — codes, pedal and throttle signals, voltage — then I check the wiring for continuity. Only once I’ve found and fixed the cause do I clear the codes.
Oleg will check the gas pedal and throttle with a scan tool, test the wiring for continuity and clear the codes after the repair. Mobile service available.
Gas pedal unresponsive
Stop, turn the engine off, wait 1–2 minutes and restart: after a random glitch the ECU may come out of limp mode. If it happens again, find the cause — don’t just clear the code.
Check the battery and fuses: with the engine off it should read about 12.6 V. A run-down battery or loose terminals make the pedal and throttle electronics glitch. The ECU fuses are listed below.
Inspect the connector on the pedal itself: is it fully seated, any corrosion or chafed wires? Check the engine ground too: a corroded ground strap also causes signal glitches.

Scan tool: the live data shows two pedal position sensors (APP1 and APP2). Press the pedal slowly to the floor: both signals should rise smoothly with no jumps or dropouts. Usually the second one is about half of the first or offset from it — what matters is that they change in step.

Multimeter: with the ignition on, each pedal sensor should have a 5 V reference and ground at the connector. With the pedal released the signal is usually about 0.5–1 V, rising smoothly to 3.5–4.5 V as you press it. Jumps, dips or dropouts at some point in the travel mean a worn pedal.
Codes: P2122–P2128 — pedal sensor input low or high, P2138 — the two pedal sensor signals disagree. The sensors are built into the pedal, so usually the whole pedal assembly is replaced.

If the pedal checks out but the car still doesn’t respond, check the throttle body: a dirty, unlearned or faulty one gives the same symptoms. Codes from other sensors, such as the MAF, also matter: the ECU limits power.
Radiator fan runs all the time

If the fan runs non-stop, even on a cold engine, the ECU has usually switched it on in fail-safe mode because it doesn’t trust the coolant temperature sensor. Common causes: a corroded temperature sensor connector (code P0116 and similar), wiring, a stuck relay or a faulty fan control module.
Don’t touch the radiator fan with your hands while the ignition is on. On many cars it can start spinning by itself, even with the engine off.

When the fan runs all the time, the temperature sensor itself isn’t always to blame. On a Volkswagen Polo with code P0116 the sensor was fine — the connector pins were corroded: I cleaned them and the fan went back to normal without replacing the sensor.
Oleg will read the codes and check the temperature sensor, wiring, relay and fan control module — even when the scan tool shows no codes. Mobile service available.
Fan runs constantly
Radiator fan won’t turn off

First rule out normal behavior: after a hot engine is shut off, the fan may run for a few more minutes, and with the A/C on it runs constantly. Turn the A/C off (A/C button; on many cars the windshield defrost mode also turns it on) and check again.
Look at the temperature gauge: if it’s above the middle, the engine really is hot and the fan is running for a reason. Check the coolant level and watch for overheating.

Read the codes and look at the coolant temperature in the live data. P0115–P0119 — temperature sensor: with this code the ECU keeps the fan on. −40 °C on the scan tool means an open circuit; 130 °C or more on a cold engine means a short.

Compare the scan tool temperature with reality: on a cold engine it should be about the outside air temperature, and 85–105 °C when warm, with no jumps. If the reading jumps or you get an implausible signal code (P0116), look for a poor contact.

Inspect the coolant temperature sensor connector (usually on the thermostat housing or the cylinder head). With the engine off, unplug it, clean the corroded pins, treat them with contact spray, plug it back in firmly and clear the code.
If the fan goes back to normal after you clear the code but the code returns later, the problem is the connector contact or the sensor wiring. Don’t rush to replace the sensor itself.
No codes? Swap the fan relay with a neighboring one with the same markings: a relay with welded contacts keeps the fan running.

Many cars have a fan control module instead of a relay — on the Chery Tiggo, for example, it’s under the left headlight. The scan tool may show no codes. If the fan starts working normally after you unplug and reconnect its connector, suspect the module.
Engine keeps running with the ignition off

You turned the key and even pulled it out, but the engine keeps running. A common cause is a worn ignition switch: the key comes out before the switch reaches the OFF position, so the ignition circuits stay on. Less often it’s the ignition switch contacts or a stuck ignition relay.

Don’t disconnect the battery terminal or flip the battery disconnect switch with the engine running: the voltage spike from the alternator can damage the control units. Don’t block the air intake with your hand or a rag — it can get sucked into the engine.

An Iveco Stralis wouldn’t shut off after a starter repair, and at first the starter was the suspect. It turned out the key came out before the switch reached OFF: the switch was worn. So I first check how the switch actually works instead of blaming the last repair.
Oleg will check the ignition switch, its contacts, the relay and the ignition circuits, and replace the switch. Mobile service available, trucks included.
Engine won’t shut off
Engine won’t shut off with the key

Put the key back in and, with a little force, turn it all the way to the off position (LOCK, OFF or 0) — past the point where the key can already come out. If the engine stops and the dash goes dark, the switch is worn.

Manual transmission, gas or diesel: set the parking brake, hold the brake pedal, press the clutch, select 4th or 5th gear and slowly let the clutch out — the engine will stall. This does no harm to the electrical system.
Gas engine: pull the fuel pump fuse or relay (below) — the engine will burn off the fuel and stall within a few seconds. Then put it back.

Electronically controlled diesel (common rail, unit injectors): pull the engine ECU fuse or power relay — the engine will stop. On a diesel with a mechanical injection pump, disconnect the wire from the fuel shutoff solenoid on the pump or move the stop lever.
Once the engine is off, look at the dash with the key out. If it’s still lit, the ignition circuits aren’t switching off: the culprit is the switch, its contacts or the ignition relay.
If the key comes out before the switch reaches OFF, the switch is worn. If it has already been repaired, it’s better to replace it entirely: yet another repair of a worn switch usually doesn’t last.
Until it’s fixed, don’t leave the car with the engine running, and don’t pull the key until the engine has stopped and the dash has gone dark.
Many trucks have an engine stop button on the engine or in the engine compartment — check the owner’s manual for its location.
On trucks the ignition feed (terminal 15) is often switched through a relay. If it sticks, the engine runs even with the key out: after stopping the engine, swap the relay for an identical good one.
Truck: many trucks have an engine stop button on the engine or in the engine compartment — check the owner’s manual for its location.

Truck: on trucks the ignition feed (terminal 15) is often switched through a relay. If it sticks, the engine runs even with the key out: after stopping the engine, swap the relay for an identical good one.
Automatic transmission shifter locked

Press the brake pedal and listen near the lever: the shift lock solenoid should click softly. If the brake lights work but there is no click, the lock isn’t getting power, a wire is broken or the solenoid has burned out. Sometimes a light tap on the console by the lever with the brake pressed frees it.

If the button on the shifter handle presses too easily, sticks or works only now and then, a plastic latch or spring inside has broken. Don’t force the lever and don’t take the shifter apart without experience — that’s how the mechanism gets broken.

If the lever started sticking after the interior was washed or water was spilled, the contacts and microswitches inside the shifter have corroded. Use the Shift Lock only to get where you’re going: it needs a diagnosis — a scan tool will show whether the transmission sees the brake and the lever position.
Transmission adaptation: how to do it yourself

Adaptation is the transmission’s learning process: it relearns the fluid pressure, shift points and engine load. It’s done after a fluid change, a transmission or valve body repair, disconnecting the battery, and when shifts get jerky. A full adaptation needs a scan tool; without one, only a partial one is possible, and not on every car.
You can try an adaptation without a computer, but it’s a limited method: I only do a full transmission relearn with proper equipment. And most importantly, adaptation is no substitute for repair.
Oleg will do a transmission adaptation with a scan tool: check for codes, reset the old values and run the relearn. Mobile service available.
Do a transmission adaptation
First read the transmission codes with a scan tool and check the fluid as the manual says. If there are codes, fix the cause first: adaptation only helps a healthy transmission without serious wear.

Warm the car up to operating temperature — preferably by driving, not idling: the transmission fluid warms up more slowly than the engine. Don’t do an adaptation on a cold car. If the scan tool shows the transmission fluid temperature, go by that.

With a scan tool: find the adaptation function in the transmission module, reset the old adaptations and run the learning procedure following the on-screen prompts. The software sets the conditions — fluid temperature, rpm, selector position — so follow them exactly.
Without a computer (partial adaptation): put the selector in D, pull away slowly and accelerate smoothly, without stabbing the gas. Drive like this for 10–20 minutes.

Then repeat with light acceleration at different speeds and take it on the highway so the transmission goes through all the gears. Don’t floor it right after a reset — that only makes the shifts worse.

If hard shifts, slipping, delayed shifts or limp mode remain after the adaptation, adaptation won’t help: that happens with worn clutch packs, low fluid pressure or a faulty solenoid. Message Oleg — he’ll tell you what to do next.
Why ECUs fail and how to protect yours

An engine control unit (ECU) rarely fails on its own — outside causes kill it. Most often it’s water, a short in the wiring, voltage spikes from an incorrect jump-start, a poor ground or a faulty alternator, welding without disconnecting the battery, vibration, a crash, and the age of the electronics.

Water kills the unit most often. After an engine wash, a Hyundai wouldn’t start: water got into the ECU connector, the pins corroded and some traces on the board rotted away — once the board was restored, the car started. And on another car, welding the rocker panels without disconnecting the battery burned out the unit’s power supply.

Oleg will check the unit’s power, grounds and communication, and if the ECU itself is at fault, he’ll repair the board. The sooner the fault is found, the better the chance of avoiding an expensive replacement.
Why ECUs fail

Signs that the unit itself is at fault: no communication with the scan tool, lots of random codes, lost spark or injection, the engine stalls for no reason. But first check the fuses, the unit’s power and ground, and its connector — they’re often to blame, not the ECU itself.

Don’t pressure-wash the engine and don’t drive through deep puddles. If the car won’t start after a wash, disconnect the negative battery terminal, unplug the ECU connector, check the pins for corrosion and dry it out.

Jump-start correctly: don’t reverse the polarity, connect the donor’s negative to engine ground, and don’t remove the battery terminals with the engine running. Don’t jump-start with a powerful booster set to a higher voltage.

Before welding on the body, disconnect the battery terminals, unplug the ECU connector if you can, and clamp the welder’s ground as close to the weld as possible. The unit may not fail right away but a few days later.

Keep an eye on charging and grounds: 13.5–14.5 V with the engine running; consistently above 15 V means overcharging. Clean and tighten the engine and body grounds: a poor ground and voltage spikes burn out the unit’s regulators and power-supply chips.

Don’t allow botched wiring: cheap alarms, twisted splices without solder, chafed harnesses. A short circuit blows the output drivers inside the ECU. Don’t flash the unit on the spot with cheap equipment: after a failed write, it stops communicating.
Kia and Hyundai: use genuine or quality ignition coils and replace the spark plugs on time. Cheap coils and worn plugs cause arcing and voltage spikes, and the damage passes down the line to the ECU.

Inspect the ECU mounting: if the rubber isolator bushings have dried out or cracked, vibration goes straight to the circuit board, causing cracks and broken solder joints. This is especially common on diesel Hyundai, Kia and Mercedes CDI. Also watch for oil and coolant leaks near the unit.

DAF 105/106: the ECU sits on the engine on rubber isolator bushings. If they’ve dried out, replace them: vibration cracks the board and the connection to the sensors drops out. The unit lasts 8–12 years or 800,000–1,500,000 km on average.
Jump-starting a truck is a common cause of ECU failure: check the polarity and jump only from a 24 V source.

Truck: dAF 105/106: the ECU sits on the engine on rubber isolator bushings. If they’ve dried out, replace them: vibration cracks the board and the connection to the sensors drops out. The unit lasts 8–12 years or 800,000–1,500,000 km on average.
Truck: jump-starting a truck is a common cause of ECU failure: check the polarity and jump only from a 24 V source.
How to check the real mileage

Usually only the odometer in the instrument cluster gets rolled back, while the real mileage stays in other modules, in the engine hours, in the wear of the interior and components, and in the service history. Compare all of these: mismatches give a rollback away.
Even if the mileage looks nice, I always check the engine hours with diagnostics — it’s one of the most honest indicators of how much the car has really been used.
Oleg will connect a scan tool, compare the mileage in every module with the odometer, check the engine hours and inspect the car before you buy. Mobile service available.
Check the real mileage
Real mileage check

Connect a scan tool and compare the mileage stored in different modules with the odometer: engine, transmission, ABS. Often only the instrument cluster is rolled back, and the real mileage stays in the other modules.

If the scan tool shows engine hours, do the math: mileage ≈ engine hours × average speed. Use 20–25 km/h for city driving and 35–40 km/h for highway driving. Example: 4,000 hours × 25 km/h ≈ 100,000 km; if the cluster shows 60,000, the odometer has been rolled back.

Check the interior: the steering wheel (worn, shiny), the pedal rubbers, the driver’s seat (sagging, worn), the buttons and switches. If the claimed mileage is 80,000–120,000 km but the interior looks tired, be suspicious.
Check the parts that wear with mileage: brake rotors and pads, shocks, play in the suspension, and the condition of the engine and transmission. Serious wear before 100,000 km is rare.

Compare the service history: the service book, work orders and receipts. Dates and mileage should go up in order: if an old receipt shows more mileage than the cluster does now, the odometer has been rolled back.
Run the VIN through online services: registration history, insurance claims, inspections. Some databases record the mileage at different points in the car’s life.
Indirect signs are red flags too: a condition too “perfect” for the car’s age, a new steering wheel or a reupholstered interior, a replaced instrument cluster. Ask the seller why they were replaced.
On trucks and heavy equipment, the scan tool shows engine hours more often. A long-haul tractor’s average speed is higher — about 40–60 km/h: 10,000 engine hours is roughly 400,000–600,000 km.
Truck: on trucks and heavy equipment, the scan tool shows engine hours more often. A long-haul tractor’s average speed is higher — about 40–60 km/h: 10,000 engine hours is roughly 400,000–600,000 km.
How to program a new key

Programming a key means pairing the chip (transponder) in the key with the car’s immobilizer. Without it, the engine won’t start or will stall after 1–2 seconds. You need it if you’ve lost a key, bought a new one, or replaced the ignition lock, the immobilizer unit or the ECU.
Always keep a spare key, and don’t buy cheap Chinese chips without testing them. If a key won’t program, I check the power supply and fuses first, and if there are codes I run diagnostics right away.
With the car’s documents, Oleg will program the key with a scan tool, restore the immobilizer and find the cause if the key won’t program. Mobile service available.
Program a new key
Key programming
Have the car’s documents ready: the registration certificate and the owner’s ID or a power of attorney. Without them, no one will program a key or give you a PIN code.

Buy a key made for your car: with the right transponder (matched by VIN or the old key’s part number) and a blade cut to your lock. Cheap untested Chinese chips are a common reason a key won’t program.
Charge the battery and check the fuses: with low voltage, programming fails and the key doesn’t get stored.

If you have a working programmed key, check the owner’s manual to see whether you can add a key yourself. On some cars, you turn the ignition on and off with the working key, quickly insert the new one and turn the ignition on again. The sequence and timing differ by make.
Some cars have a service learning mode: you turn on the ignition and press a specific button combination. The sequence is different for each make — take it only from the manual for your model.

No working key, a car built after 2010, or a German car — you’ll need a scan tool and a PIN code. The PIN is issued by VIN only to the owner with documents. Message Oleg: he’ll connect the scan tool, enter the PIN and program the keys.
If you’ve lost a key, ask for it to be erased from memory during programming. On many cars, programming erases all keys and re-stores only the ones you have with you, so bring every key.
After programming, test every key: the engine starts and doesn’t stall after 1–2 seconds. On many cars the fob buttons are programmed separately — check that they lock and unlock the doors.
How to wire an electric air conditioner

An electric (parking) air conditioner doesn’t need an engine-driven compressor or refrigerant lines, but it draws a lot of current, especially when the compressor starts. The key to the install is power: heavy-gauge wires straight to the battery, a fuse near the battery, a power relay and a good ground.
A thin wire, a connection to the cigarette lighter or factory wiring, or a wire with no fuse near the battery will overheat and can catch fire. Disconnect the negative battery terminal before wiring.

Before installing, I check the alternator and clean the battery terminals. The most common mistakes are wires that are too thin, a poor ground, no relay and cheap connectors, so I never skimp on wiring and fuses.
Oleg will check the alternator and battery, pick the right wires and fuse, and wire up the A/C with a relay and battery protection — the power side is best left to him. Mobile service available.
Wire an electric A/C
Electric A/C installation

Choose the location: a rooftop unit for a truck, van or camper; for a car, under or behind a seat or on the rear wall. The surface must be solid, and the unit must not vibrate, touch any wiring or press against the body metal.
Route the drain tube outside with no kinks, and protect the edges of the hole from rust: without a drain, condensation will run into the cabin. Seal the holes in the roof and body.
Pick the power wires by the A/C’s current rating from the manual: up to 30 A — at least 6 mm², 40–60 A — 10–16 mm². The longer the run, the thicker the wire. The negative wire must be the same size.

Run the positive straight from the battery through a fuse and a power relay. Mount the fuse as close to the positive terminal as possible, rated as the A/C manual specifies. Run the wire in split loom, and use a rubber grommet where it passes through the body.

Connect the negative to the battery negative or to clean body metal under a factory bolt, with a ring terminal. Crimp the terminals with a crimper and don’t use cheap connectors: a poor ground and a loose contact heat up.

Protect the battery from going flat: when parked, the A/C runs off the battery. Turn on the low-voltage cutoff in the controller and pick a higher threshold so there’s enough charge left to start. For long running while parked, an auxiliary battery is added.

Before the first start, measure the voltage: about 12.5 V with the engine off, 13.5–14.5 V with it running. Switch on the A/C: the voltage shouldn’t drop much, the air should be cold and the fans should run.

After a few minutes of running, feel the wires and terminals and sniff for odors. If a wire or terminal is getting hot or you smell hot wiring, the wire is too thin or there’s a bad connection: switch the A/C off and redo it.
Trucks and heavy equipment on 24 V: get a 24 V unit — at the same power it draws half the current. Check the alternator before installing: you may need a bigger alternator or an auxiliary battery.

Brake air pressure
Air pressure in the brake system is low — the brakes may not work properly.
Don’t move off. If it comes on while driving, stop smoothly in a safe place and turn on the hazard lights.
Let the engine run until the pressure builds up to normal and the light goes out. If it doesn’t build up, listen for hissing — that’s how you find the leak.
If the pressure drops again or the compressor won’t build it up, don’t drive on: call a mechanic.
Cab not locked
The cab didn’t latch after tilting, or the latch sensor is faulty. Driving with an unlocked cab is dangerous.
Don’t move off. Lower the cab all the way as described in the owner’s manual and make sure the latches have engaged.
If the cab is down but the light stays on, check the cab latch switch and its connector. On some trucks it also keeps the starter from engaging.
Low oil level
The engine oil is below normal — time to top up. It’s not as urgent as the red oil can, but don’t put it off.
Park on level ground, switch off the engine and check the level with the dipstick after 5–10 minutes.
If it’s below MIN, add oil of the viscosity stated in the owner’s manual until the level is between MIN and MAX. Don’t overfill.
If the oil goes down quickly, look for leaks or oil burning. If the red oil can comes on, switch off the engine at once.
Low coolant level
The coolant in the expansion tank is low. If you don’t top it up, the engine will overheat.
If the temperature gauge is rising or the symbol is red, stop and switch off the engine, as with overheating.
With the engine cold, open the tank and add the same type of coolant until the level is between MIN and MAX. Don’t open it hot — steam will scald you.
If the level drops again, look for a leak: hoses, radiator, water pump, heater core.
EPC (VW, Audi, Skoda)
A fault in the engine management: the throttle body, gas pedal or brake switch. The engine may go into limp mode.
If the engine pulls as usual, drive to a shop and read the trouble codes with a scan tool.
If the engine has lost power or the rpm is hunting, slow down and don’t drive far: power is limited.
Common causes are a dirty throttle body, the gas pedal sensor and the brake pedal switch. Check that the brake lights work.
EPC light is on
Low washer fluid
The washer fluid reservoir is running low.
Top up the reservoir under the hood — its cap has a windshield-and-spray symbol. In winter use only winter washer fluid.
If the reservoir is full but the light stays on, check the level sensor in the reservoir and its connector.
