Exterior bulb failure
The control unit sees that one of the exterior bulbs is out: a headlight, brake light, parking light, turn signal or license plate light.
Turn on the lights and walk around the car to find what’s out. Check the brake lights with a helper or by the reflection in a window.
Replace the burnt-out bulb with one of the same type and wattage.
If LED bulbs were fitted, the control unit often treats them as burnt out. Use CAN-bus LED bulbs or a load resistor.
An exterior bulb is out
Rear fog light
The rear fog light is on — a bright red light at the rear.
Use it only in fog, snow or heavy rain. Turn it off in clear weather: it dazzles drivers behind you and makes your brake lights harder to see.
Electric parking brake
A fault in the electric parking brake (EPB): it may not apply or may not release.
When parked, play it safe: leave it in gear or in P, and chock a wheel on a slope.
Switch the engine off and restart: after a voltage dip the fault sometimes clears. Check the battery.
If it stays, it needs a diagnosis: the code will show whether it’s the caliper motor, a wire or the switch.
Key not detected
The car can’t find the smart key inside. The engine won’t stall while driving, but it may not restart once you stop.
Make sure the key is in the car. Keep it away from your phone, other keys and metal — they interfere with the signal.
Hold the key right against the Start button and press it: many cars will start this way even with a dead key battery.
Replace the key battery. If that doesn’t help, try the spare key.
Key battery low
The key battery is almost dead — soon the car won’t be able to detect the key.
Replace the battery: usually a CR2032 or CR2025 — the type is printed on the battery itself.
Until you replace it, start the car by holding the key right against the Start button.
Key fob battery
Steering lock (ESCL)
The electronic steering column lock is faulty: the steering may not unlock, and the car won’t start.
Rock the steering wheel left and right while pressing Start or turning the key — the lock may be stuck.
Check the battery: with low voltage the steering lock often doesn’t work.
If it keeps happening, the steering lock and its power supply need a diagnosis.
Warning
The triangle with “!” comes on with a message on the instrument cluster display that says what’s wrong. On Toyota and Lexus it’s red.
Read the message on the cluster display and look it up in the owner’s manual. Many cars keep past messages in the cluster menu.
If a red symbol is also on or the car behaves oddly, stop and find out why.
If there’s no message but the symbol stays on, it needs a scan tool diagnosis.
Reduced power (turtle)
The control unit has limited power to protect the engine, transmission or hybrid battery. The car drives but accelerates poorly.
Drive gently, with no passing or hard acceleration, and get to a shop.
Hybrid or EV: the symbol can come on when the battery is nearly empty, overheated or very cold. Charge it or wait.
If it doesn’t go away, read the trouble codes with a scan tool: they’ll show the cause.

Rear window defroster
The rear window defroster is on. It usually switches itself off after 10–20 minutes.
If the glass doesn’t clear or clears in stripes, check the heating grid lines and the contacts at the edges of the glass: they often get torn off.
If it doesn’t heat at all, check the defroster fuse and relay.
Passenger airbag off
The front passenger airbag is switched off. That’s correct when a rear-facing child seat is in the front seat.
If an adult is sitting there and the symbol is on, check the airbag switch: it’s usually key-operated, on the end of the dashboard or in the glove box.
If the airbag switches itself off with an adult passenger, the seat occupant sensor needs a diagnosis.
Ice warning
It’s about +3 °C or colder outside: the road may be icy, especially on bridges and in the shade.
Slow down, leave more following distance and brake early and gently.
AWD/4WD fault
The AWD control unit has found a fault or the coupling has overheated: the car may drive on one axle only. The same symbol in green just means 4WD is engaged.
Don’t spin the wheels. Stop, let the coupling cool for 10–15 minutes and restart.
Check that all four tires match: different sizes or uneven wear upset the drive system.
If it stays on, it needs a diagnosis: common culprits are a wheel speed sensor, the coupling or the mode switch.
Differential lock
The differential lock is on: the wheels on the axle turn together. It’s only for off-road and slippery ground.
Turn the lock off on pavement: with it the vehicle turns poorly and the tires and drivetrain wear faster.
If the symbol flashes, the lock hasn’t engaged or disengaged yet. Drive slowly straight ahead; if that doesn’t help, check the lock sensor and actuator.
Air suspension
An air suspension fault: the vehicle may sag or not hold its ride height.
If the vehicle has sagged, don’t drive fast or over rough roads: you can damage the suspension and the underbody.
Start the engine and wait a few minutes: the compressor should raise the body. If it doesn’t, check the compressor fuse and relay.
If it sags overnight, air is leaking somewhere: an air spring, the lines or the valves. It needs a diagnosis.
Start-stop unavailable
The start-stop system is switched off with its button, temporarily unavailable or faulty. You can keep driving.
The system won’t stop the engine until the battery is charged and the engine is warm, or while strong heating or A/C is on — that’s normal.
If the symbol stays on all the time, check the battery. Start-stop cars use AGM or EFB batteries, and a new one often has to be registered with a scan tool.
If that doesn’t help, it needs a diagnosis: often the battery sensor on the negative terminal is at fault.
The engine air filter is clogged: the engine is short of air, power drops and fuel use goes up.
Replace the air filter and log it in the “Maintenance” section.
If the filter is new but the light stays on, check the restriction (vacuum) sensor on the filter housing and its connector.
Power take-off (PTO)
The PTO is engaged: the engine is driving the pump of the dump body, crane or other equipment.
Disengage the PTO before driving off unless the owner’s manual allows driving with it engaged.
If you’ve disengaged it but the symbol stays on, check the PTO engagement sensor and its wire.
Trailer ABS/EBS
A trailer ABS or EBS fault: the trailer brakes still work, but the wheels may lock under hard braking.
Brake early and gently, especially on slippery roads and downhill.
Check the ABS/EBS connector between the tractor and trailer (ISO 7638): fully plugged in, contacts not corroded, cable intact.
If it stays on, the trailer needs a diagnosis: often a wheel speed sensor or the modulator power supply.
A turn signal or the hazards are on. If it flashes twice as fast as usual, a turn signal bulb on that side has burned out.
If it flashes fast, find which bulb is out — front, rear or the side repeater on the fender — and replace it.
If it doesn’t flash at all or stays on solid, check the turn signal fuse and flasher relay, and if an alarm is fitted, its wiring.
Turn signals flash fast
Low beam
The low beam headlights are on.
If the symbol is on but a headlight is dark, check that headlight’s bulb and fuse.
Parking lights
The parking lights are on: the front and rear marker lights and the license plate light.
Turn them off when parked: overnight they can drain the battery.
Press the brake pedal
The car is asking you to press the brake: without it, it won’t start with the Start button or the shifter won’t come out of P.
Press the brake pedal all the way and hold it while you start the engine or move the shifter.
If you’re holding the brake and the symbol stays on, check whether the brake lights work: often it’s the brake light fuse or the pedal switch.
“Press brake” is on and the shifter won’t leave P
Press the clutch
A manual car is asking you to press the clutch — to start the engine, or for start-stop to restart it.
Press the clutch pedal all the way down and start the engine.
If the clutch is down but the symbol stays on and the starter is silent, check the clutch pedal switch and its connector.
Won’t start: “press clutch” is on
Start-stop active
The start-stop system shut the engine off while you’re stopped to save fuel. That’s normal.
The engine restarts by itself when you release the brake (automatic) or press the clutch (manual). You can turn the system off with the button marked A.
Lane keeping assist
The system watches the lane markings and steers back or warns you if the car drifts out of the lane. A yellow or gray symbol means it can’t see the lines or is off.
If it can’t see the lines, clean the windshield in front of the camera by the mirror. It switches off by itself in snow, rain and on worn markings.
After a windshield replacement, the camera has to be calibrated at a shop.
Hill descent control (HDC)
Hill descent control is on: on a steep downhill the car brakes by itself and holds a low speed.
Flashing on a descent means the system is braking — that’s normal. The brakes may make noise while it works.
Turn the system off with its button on level roads. If it’s yellow, the system is unavailable or faulty.
Auto Hold
Auto Hold is on: after you stop, the car holds the brakes itself, so you can take your foot off the pedal.
To pull away, just press the gas — the brake releases by itself.
If it won’t turn on, check that the driver’s seat belt is buckled and the door is closed: many cars won’t enable it otherwise.
Engine brake / retarder
The engine (exhaust) brake or retarder is on: the truck slows down without wearing the brake linings.
Use it on long downhill grades so the brakes don’t overheat. Engage it carefully on slippery roads: the truck can skid.
If the symbol is on but there’s no braking effect, check the switch, the engine brake solenoid valve and its wiring.
Engine cold
The coolant is still cold. The symbol goes out once the engine warms up.
For the first few minutes drive gently and keep the revs low.
If it’s still on after 15–20 minutes of driving and the heater blows cold, the thermostat is probably stuck open.

After a crash or a hard hit: the fuel or power safety cutoff has tripped

In a crash, or after hitting a deep pothole, a bump or a curb, the car shuts off the fuel pump for safety — so a damaged fuel line doesn’t start a fire. On some cars a crash also fires a pyrotechnic fuse at the battery and cuts all power. It’s a safety feature, not a fault: if there’s no fuel leak, it can be reset.
Inspect the car first: if you smell gasoline or it’s wet or dripping underneath, don’t turn the pump on and don’t start it — call a tow truck. If the airbags deployed, take it to a mechanic.

The starter cranks but the engine won’t start and you don’t hear the fuel pump prime — find the inertia fuel pump shutoff switch and press its button until it clicks. It’s usually a red or black button on top of a small unit.

Where to look: most often in the front passenger footwell behind the side trim panel or behind the glove box; sometimes under the steering wheel by the pedals behind a panel, under the hood on the firewall, or in the trunk behind the side trim. The exact spot is in the owner’s manual, in the section on the emergency fuel shutoff.

Examples: Ford Focus — on the right under the dash or behind the right side panel in the passenger footwell; Ford Fiesta — in the passenger footwell behind the glove box, on some hatchbacks in the trunk behind the right trim; Ford Transit 2000–2014 and Transit Connect before 2013 — on the left by the pedals behind the lower panel; Transit from 2014, Transit Custom, Transit Connect from 2013 and Transit Courier — behind the glove box; Jaguar — on the left ahead of the door pillar under the dash, behind a trim panel with a finger hole. Some Lada, UAZ and Daewoo cars have one too — check the manual.
After pressing it, turn the ignition off for 10–15 seconds and back on: the pump should hum for 2–3 seconds. Then start the engine.

No button — on many modern cars the control unit itself cuts the pump on a crash signal from the airbag module. Turn the ignition off, open and close the driver’s door, wait a minute and turn it back on. If that doesn’t help, it needs a scan tool: the airbag module keeps a crash record that a mechanic clears, and sometimes the module is replaced.

The car is completely dead, or the starter won’t crank with a charged battery — check the pyrotechnic fuse at the battery positive terminal or in the power fuse box next to it. BMWs with the battery in the trunk have one, for example: after an impact the terminal fires apart, the lights and radio may still work, but the engine won’t start. A fired pyro fuse can’t be reset — it’s replaced, then the airbag codes are cleared with a scan tool.
If the airbags or the pyro fuse fired, or the wiring or fuel lines are damaged, it needs diagnostics: Oleg will check the airbag module, clear the crash records and find what else the impact damaged.
The switch can trip without a crash — from a hard hit into a pothole or a curb, or while loading onto a tow truck. Before hunting for a complex fault, press it: it takes a minute.
If you smell gasoline, don’t press anything and don’t start the engine.
The motorcycle fell and won’t start: the tip-over sensor has tripped
Most fuel-injected motorcycles have a tip-over (bank angle) sensor: when the bike falls, it kills the engine and cuts the fuel pump and ignition to prevent a fire.
If you smell gasoline or fuel is leaking, don’t start it until the leak is fixed.
Stand the motorcycle up on its wheels or stand.
Turn the ignition off for 10–15 seconds and back on: you should hear the fuel pump prime.
Check the engine kill switch on the right handlebar — it often gets knocked in a fall.
Still won’t start — inspect the tip-over sensor connector (usually under the seat) and the fuses, and look for wires broken in the fall.
After a fall, a bike often won’t start because of the handlebar kill switch — check it first.

Automatic shifter in N
Is it an automatic — a conventional automatic, CVT or automated manual? Set the parking brake, press the brake pedal, move the shifter to N and try to start it again.
Automatic: the starter cranks in N
Automatic: silent in N too
Manual transmission
Automatic: no crank in P — start it in N

On an automatic, the starter cranks only in P and N — the transmission range sensor (neutral safety switch, inhibitor) allows it. Its contacts burn and wear over time: in P the starter circuit stops closing, while in N it still closes. That’s why the car often starts in neutral.
Start in N only with the parking brake set and the brake pedal pressed: in neutral the car can roll.
Set the parking brake, press the brake pedal, move the shifter to N and start the engine.
Silent in N too — put the lever back in P, wiggle it slightly within P and try again: a burnt contact sometimes closes with a small shift.
Look at the instrument cluster: does the letter on the display match the lever position? If another letter or none shows in P, the sensor is out of adjustment or the shifter cable has stretched.
If it starts in N, drive as usual. When you leave the car, put the lever in P and set the parking brake.
Won’t start in P or N — check the starter fuse and relay (below) and the range sensor connector on the transmission for corrosion and moisture.
A scan tool may show a range sensor or P/N switch code — for example, P0705 or P0850.

If it starts only in N, have the range sensor checked: over time it will stop allowing a start in N too. It also tells the transmission control unit which gear is selected. Oleg will check the sensor, the shifter cable and the starter interlock circuit, and adjust or replace the sensor.
A common story: on an automatic the starter is silent in P but cranks in N, and the car starts. The range sensor contacts have burnt. You can get to a shop like this, but don’t put off the repair.
Parking brake set, foot on the brake, no one near the car.
Automatic: shift to N and try again — with a burnt range sensor the starter often won’t crank in P but will in N.

When the battery goes flat
When does the battery go flat?
Overnight or after a day parked
After a few days parked
While driving, or the battery light is on
Aftermarket equipment
Does the car have any equipment that wasn’t fitted at the factory? A remote-start alarm, an aftermarket head unit, a dashcam, a GPS tracker, an amplifier, extra lights.
Yes, there is
Not sure — I bought it used
No, everything is factory
If there’s aftermarket equipment — an alarm, head unit, dashcam, tracker — start with it: disconnect it overnight and see whether the battery still goes flat. It’s the most common cause.

Wait for the modules to go to sleep — anywhere from a few minutes to an hour; don’t open the doors during that time. Ideally the current is 0.06 A (60 mA) or less. Noticeably more, say 0.1–0.2 A, means some module isn’t going to sleep.
Flat overnight: start with the aftermarket equipment

When the battery goes flat overnight or within a day, usually some module isn’t going to sleep and keeps drawing current. Most often it’s equipment that wasn’t fitted at the factory: an alarm, an aftermarket head unit, a dashcam, a tracker, an amplifier. Start there, and check the factory modules after.

While the multimeter is connected in series, don’t turn on the ignition or start the engine — the meter will burn out. Only disconnect an alarm that blocks starting if you know how to reconnect it: without it the car may not start.
Unplug everything powered from the cigarette lighter and USB overnight: dashcam, chargers, tracker, compressor. If the battery is fine in the morning, the culprit is one of them.
Aftermarket head unit: turn off the ignition and lock the car. The head unit and its button lighting should go dark. If they don’t, it’s been wired to constant positive and never switches off.
Remote-start alarm: check whether it goes off by itself, or relays click under the dash, while the car sits locked.

Check the lights that should switch off on their own: glovebox, trunk, dome lights, vanity mirror lights in the sun visors. You can’t see the glovebox light with the lid shut: put your phone inside recording video, close it for a minute, then watch the recording.
Even a single 5 W bulb draws about 0.4 A — roughly 10 Ah over a day. On a cold or undercharged battery that’s enough for the starter to barely turn over in the morning.

Measure the parasitic draw. Turn off the ignition and all equipment, and close the doors. Remove the negative terminal and connect the multimeter — DC amps, red lead in the 10 A jack — between the battery’s negative post and the removed terminal.

Wait for the modules to go to sleep — anywhere from a few minutes to an hour — without opening the doors. Ideally the current is 0.06 A (60 mA) or less. If it’s higher, disconnect the aftermarket equipment one item at a time (its power connector or fuse) and watch the meter: when the current drops to normal, you’ve found what isn’t sleeping.

With the aftermarket equipment disconnected and the current still high, the problem is in the factory modules or the wiring. Pull the fuses one at a time: whichever one makes the current drop, look in that circuit. Sometimes a faulty alternator is what’s drawing the current.
Of the add-on equipment on machinery, check the tracker, two-way radio, parking heater and inverter first.
Of the add-on equipment on a truck, check the tracker, two-way radio, parking heater and inverter first.

Aftermarket first, factory second. Most often what keeps a car from sleeping is something added later: an alarm, an aftermarket head unit, a dashcam. Disconnect it overnight — by morning you’ll know whether that’s the cause.
Oleg will find which module isn’t going to sleep: he’ll measure the key-off draw, check the aftermarket equipment, then the factory modules and the alternator.
The alternator isn’t charging the battery

If the battery goes flat while you drive, or the battery light is on with the engine running, the alternator isn’t charging. The car is running on what’s left in the battery and will stall before long.
If the alternator belt has snapped, don’t keep driving: on many cars the same belt drives the water pump, and the engine will overheat quickly.
Switch off everything you don’t need — window and seat heaters, the heater fan, music — and drive to a shop without shutting the engine off: if you stop it, it may not start again.
Look at the alternator belt: is it intact and tight, and is it squealing?

If you have a voltmeter, measure at the battery terminals with the engine running. Normal is 13.5–14.8 V. Below 13.5 V the alternator isn’t charging. Above 15 V it’s overcharging: the voltage regulator is faulty.
Inspect the battery terminals and the thick cable from the alternator: a corroded or loose connection also causes undercharging.
If the battery is more than 4–5 years old, load-test it: an old one may not hold a charge even with a healthy alternator.
For a 24 V system, normal with the engine running is 27.2–28.8 V.
Oleg will check the charging under load, the alternator and its wiring.

The battery kept going flat even after a full charge: at rest the car was drawing about 14 A. The control modules were disconnected one by one — they weren’t the cause. A faulty alternator was drawing the current; after it was replaced, the draw returned to normal.

Choosing a replacement ECU
ECU replaced: pairing it with the immobilizer

The engine control unit (ECU) “knows” its own immobilizer and keys. A new unit, or one from another car, doesn’t: the engine won’t start or stalls after 1–2 seconds, and the immobilizer light is on or flashing. After a replacement the unit must be paired with the immobilizer. But first, the most important thing: check that the new unit’s markings match the old one.
If the markings don’t match, pairing won’t help: the car may start, but the unit won’t work correctly. Compare the labels first — you can check the numbers below.

Compare the labels on the old and the new unit: part number, hardware number (HW) and software number (SW). The part number and hardware must match, and so must the engine, the gearbox (manual or automatic), the year and the market of the car.

If they don’t match, don’t fit that unit even if the car starts: the idle will hunt, fault codes will appear, the A/C, cooling fan or cruise control may not work, and an automatic gearbox will shift incorrectly.
Take photos of both labels and don’t throw the old unit away: if it’s intact, a technician can transfer the data from it for pairing.

Before pairing, check the connectors and power: the connector is clicked fully home, the pins are clean and the battery is charged. Low voltage makes pairing fail — connect a battery charger while the work is done.

Pairing is done with a scan tool: on some makes with a PIN code issued by VIN to the owner with documents, on others with dealer equipment. A unit from another car is prepared for pairing first. Many cars also need the keys re-programmed at the same time — bring the car’s documents and all the keys.
Don’t disable the immobilizer or install “immo-off” software: the car is left with no theft protection, and such software often runs with faults.
After pairing, run the adaptations: throttle body and idle, gearbox adaptation on an automatic, and on a diesel write the injector codes if the unit needs them. Then clear the fault codes.

Check the result: the engine starts with every key and doesn’t stall, the idle is steady, there are no fault codes, the rev counter, cooling fan and A/C work, and on the road so do the speedometer and gear changes.

When it’s replaced, the engine unit is configured for the vehicle with dealer software: VIN, engine and chassis parameters. Compare the unit number on the label and the software version — they decide which settings get written.

The most important thing when replacing the unit is that the label and markings match the unit you’re fitting. Otherwise it won’t work correctly, even if the car starts. And after the replacement the unit must be paired with the immobilizer.
Oleg will compare the unit markings, pair the ECU with the immobilizer using a scan tool (with the car’s documents) and run the adaptations. Mobile service is available.
How to choose a replacement ECU

Only a unit with the same markings as the old one should be fitted. A similar unit “from the same car” but with a different number may start the engine, yet it won’t work correctly. First compare the labels, then buy, and after fitting, pair it with the immobilizer.
Find the old unit and photograph the whole label: part number, hardware number (HW), software number (SW) and the unit’s maker (Bosch, Continental, Denso, Delphi and others).
Look for a unit with the same part and hardware numbers. Even one letter at the end of the number means a different version: fit it only if a technician confirms compatibility from the catalogue.
Check the donor car too: same engine, gearbox (manual or automatic), year and market. Units for different markets and trim levels look identical, but the software inside differs.
Ask the seller for a photo of this exact unit’s label and compare the numbers before paying. Don’t buy from a photo of a “similar” unit or on the word “it’s from the same car”.
If the software number (SW) differs but the part and hardware match, the unit may fit, but a technician has to write the original software for your car into it.
Inspect the unit: the case hasn’t been opened and has no water marks, the connector and pins are intact and not corroded. Agree on a return in case the unit doesn’t fit or won’t pair.
After fitting, the unit is paired with the immobilizer using a scan tool and the adaptations are run — without that the engine won’t start or will stall after 1–2 seconds.

The EV shows no signs of life: the 12 V battery is flat — how to jump-start it

If the screen won’t turn on, the doors won’t open with the fob and the car doesn’t respond, it’s almost always the ordinary 12 V battery that’s flat, not the big battery. The 12 V battery wakes the control units and connects the high-voltage battery. That’s the only one you jump-start — from a jump starter or another car, just like a regular car.
Only the 12 V system is jump-started. Don’t touch the orange cables and connectors — they carry high voltage. A 24 V jump starter will destroy the electronics.
If the car is on charge, unplug the charging cable. Switch off the lights, heating and everything else you can.

Open the hood or front trunk. If it only opens with a button and there’s no power, look for the emergency method in the owner’s manual. For example, on a Tesla Model 3 a red and a black wire are tucked behind the front tow-eye cover: apply 12 V from a jump starter and the hood latch releases. Keep it connected for no more than 30 seconds.

Find the 12 V battery or the jump-start terminals. On some cars the battery is under the hood; on others it’s in the trunk or under the floor, with a separate “+” terminal and a ground bolt brought out under the hood. On a Tesla Model 3 the “+” terminal is under the service panel and a red cover, and ground is the bolt next to the brake fluid reservoir.
Connect the cables: red to “+”, black to ground (a bolt on the body or the ground terminal), not to the negative of the flat battery. The cables must not touch each other or other parts.
Turn on the jump starter or start the donor car and wait a few minutes. Then press the brake and the Start button, or tap the screen — the screen may take a few minutes to boot.

READY is on — the car has powered up. Disconnect the cables: black first, then red. Don’t switch the car off straight away: in READY the 12 V battery recharges from the big battery, and you don’t need to press the accelerator.

Some Kia and Hyundai hybrids have no separate 12 V battery but a 12 V battery reset button instead: press it and switch the car on within 15 seconds. Check your owner’s manual to see whether your car has one.
Only jump-start other cars from an EV if the manufacturer allows it. Tesla, for example, explicitly forbids it for the Model 3: it can damage the car.
If the battery went flat on its own, have it tested: after a deep discharge it often doesn’t hold charge well. A dashcam and other always-on devices also drain the 12 V system while parked.
Oleg will come with a jump starter, find the terminals on your model, test the 12 V battery and find what is draining it. Mobile service is available.
The EV’s big battery is empty: it can’t be jump-started

If the screen turns on but the car shows 0% and won’t drive, the traction (high-voltage) battery is empty. It can’t be jump-started from another car or a jump starter: they supply 12 V, while the battery works at hundreds of volts. It has to be charged — on the spot, or by taking the car to a charger on a tow truck.

Don’t tow an EV on a rope with its wheels on the ground: the turning wheels spin the electric motor, which generates current and can overheat, even to the point of fire. Don’t open the high-voltage battery or touch the orange cables.

If there’s a 230 V socket nearby, plug in the portable charger if one came with the car. A household socket charges slowly — a few kilometres of range per hour — but that’s enough to reach a charging station. Use a sound, earthed socket, with no extension cords or multi-plugs.
Find the nearest charging station in the car’s app or a charging network’s app and check whether the range you’ve gained is enough.
Find out whether there’s a mobile charging service in your city — a portable station comes to the car.
Otherwise call a flatbed tow truck. If there’s no flatbed, all wheels must be off the ground: a wheel lift plus wheel dollies.
To winch the car onto the flatbed, switch on transport mode (Tow Mode on a Tesla). It needs 12 V power — if the 12 V battery is flat too, jump-start it first.
You can push the car a couple of metres by hand in neutral with the parking brake off — no more than 10 metres and at walking pace.
To avoid this happening again, don’t drive down to zero. In winter the range is noticeably shorter — charge in good time.
If the car won’t charge or won’t power up after charging, Oleg will check the 12 V system and the high-voltage system with a scan tool.

Shift to P and press the brake. Touch the ENGINE START STOP button with the Toyota emblem side of the key — you’ll hear a beep and the ignition turns on. Then press the button while holding the brake. On the 2004–2009 Prius the key goes into the slot below the start button. The mechanical key inside the fob opens the door.
Same as Toyota: brake, touch the start button with the emblem side of the key, press the button after the beep (according to owners — we didn’t find the official text, check your model’s manual).

Holding the brake, press the Engine Start/Stop button with the smart key itself. The mechanical key is hidden in the fob; the driver’s door lock is under the handle cover: press the button under the handle and pry the cover off with the key.
Holding the brake, press the ENGINE START/STOP button with the key itself, holding it at a right angle to the button. Don’t hold the button longer than 10 seconds.
Shift to P (manual: neutral with the clutch pressed) and press the brake. Touch the start button with the key — you’ll hear a beep. Within 10 seconds press the button while holding the brake.
Hold the brake. While the green indicator on the start button is flashing, touch the button with the back of the key, lock button facing up. When the indicator stays on, press the button.

Press START — the button flashes for about 30 seconds. While it flashes, touch the centre of the button with the H-logo side of the key, fob buttons facing you. After the beep press the brake and START (without the brake only ACC turns on).

According to owners: on newer Outlanders press START with the back of the key; on earlier ones insert the key into the slot (in the glovebox or console). We didn’t find the official text — check your model’s manual.
According to owners: press the key against the start button with its buttons facing you; after the beep press the button while holding the brake. We didn’t find the official text — check the manual.

Tiguan (5N): shift to P, press the start button and immediately hold the key to the right side of the steering column cover. Models with a slot: insert the key into the slot. On the Golf and newer models the spot is often by the nearest cupholder (according to owners).
Octavia A7: press the start button with the key itself or hold the key to the button blade-first. On the Octavia A8 put the key in the cupholder nearest the driver, buttons up (according to owners).
Malibu: put the fob in the pocket in the centre console and start as usual. Traverse: in the armrest compartment. Tahoe: the console pocket, on newer ones the cupholder (according to owners).

Jolion: put the key in the marked spot in the front cupholder and start as usual.
Coolray: according to owners, the emergency start zone is at the bottom of the armrest. We didn’t find the official text — check the manual.
CS75: according to owners, lay the key flat on the start button, wait for the green indicator and press the button. We didn’t find the official text — check the manual.

Doesn’t detect the key and won’t start. We switched the ignition on by holding the key against the mark under the steering column. The fuses are intact, but the BCM doesn’t communicate (U0140) — next, check its power, ground and wiring.

Won’t start, the fuel pump isn’t running; the owner had already replaced the pump — no luck. With direct power the pump ran, and the fuses and relays were fine: the car alarm was cutting the power. We removed the block and it started.

Jerked while driving, thick black smoke came out, it stalled and won’t start. No codes — we found a leaking high-pressure injector. We recommended replacing the injector and the oil, and not trying to start it until it’s repaired.

The central locking won’t open the doors. The door wiring and electronics are fine — the lock relay inside the Body Control module had failed. We removed the module and resoldered the relay; the locks work again.
After the battery terminal was disconnected, it starts and stalls right away, no codes. The throttle body turned out to be dirty — after cleaning and a throttle adaptation the idle came back.

Won’t start, Security is flashing, the fan spins as soon as the ignition is on, and the scan tool can’t see the engine ECU. The fuses and grounds show no obvious damage — we recommended checking power and grounds at the ECU connector.

The starter clicks, won’t start. About 10 V with the ignition on, dropping to 7 V when cranking; charging 14,2 V — normal. We recommended replacing the battery: one successful start doesn’t mean the fault is gone.

The scan tool can’t see the engine, transmission or instrument cluster; the cluster is dead and doesn’t show the mileage. On the bench the modules communicated — we found an implausible CAN bus signal; we ran a duplicate wire for that section and everything worked.

The central locking doesn’t work. The cause was chafed wires in the harness between the door and the body. We replaced the damaged sections and the locking worked; the lock itself and the modules didn’t need replacing.

When cold, the starter won’t crank; it starts after about 30 minutes of trying, then it’s fine all day. The culprit was the starter relay under the left headlight near the bumper — after replacing it, the problem didn’t come back.
The revs hunt, the engine stalls, code P017100 — lean mixture. The live data points to the fuel system: we recommended checking the high-pressure pump, injectors, filters and fuel pressure.

After a throttle body cleaning at another shop, it won’t hold idle. Adaptation didn’t help — under the covers we found a hose that hadn’t been put back. We fitted it and the revs are normal; for the lean mixture we advised checking the fuel system.

Check Engine, 8 EVAP entries: P24507E, P04419C, P142100, P142300. The purge valve, canister pump and sensors are fine, but the car had been in a collision — we recommended a leak search: EVAP system sealing and vacuum lines.

Wouldn’t start, mileage 9 600 km. The EPB, ESC, ICU and turn signal codes were in History status — not the cause. We found a poor power contact at the clamping nut of the underhood fuse box: we cleaned and tightened it, and the problem was gone.

The starter won’t crank, the selector is in D, but the position on the dash doesn’t change. The lock washer (retainer) had come off the selector cable at the transmission. We restored the cable retention — the gears shift and the engine starts.

After an automatic transmission oil change the shifts aren’t smooth, no codes. We reset the transmission adaptations to factory values and ran the adaptation again — the shifts became smooth and the jerks disappeared.

Something crackled under the hood and the car stopped starting. The battery had dropped to 6,1 V — we jump-started it and it ran. Charging right after the start was 13,4 V, and after topping up the battery, 14,0 V: the alternator is fine.

After body work the cooling fan didn’t work — the fan connector wasn’t pushed all the way in. Later the car stalled with no charging: the charging circuit fuse had once been repaired with solder, and the solder joint had come loose.

After a radiator replacement the A/C fan didn’t come on and the temperature gauge jumped around. Wires had been pulled out of the fan connector — we repaired them; the temperature sensor was spinning in its holder — a sensor defect.

With the ignition on, the dash lights didn’t come on and it wouldn’t start. Three fuses had blown: the car had been jump-started before that — probably with the polarity reversed. We replaced the fuses, power came back and the car started.

The power windows stopped working. The fuses are fine — the window control module was faulty: we restored its power stage and resoldered components. The window mechanisms themselves didn’t need replacing.

Won’t start, no spark — the ignition module was faulty. The owner replaced it himself but mounted it incorrectly on the distributor housing, and the ECU output transistor burned out. We repaired the ECU and secured the module — there’s spark.

The alarm stopped working and the car ended up immobilized. The cause was an internal fault in the alarm module. We disconnected the faulty alarm, restored the wiring and removed the starting blocks — the car started.

The temperature readings jump: too high one moment, dropping sharply the next; codes P0125, P0171, P0420. The coolant temperature sensor was turning in its base — it needs replacing; for P0171 and P0420 a fuel system check is recommended.

After off-roading, codes in almost every module. After clearing, only the AWD coupling codes remained (U011487 and others) — the coupling connector was damaged and its latch broken. We repaired the connector and the codes went away.

Misfiring, vibration, Check Engine: P030400 and P030000. We moved the coil from cylinder 3 to cylinder 4 — the code stayed on cylinder 4. The culprit was the cylinder 4 spark plug, even though the set had been replaced a few thousand km earlier.

Starts in the morning, but after warming up and being switched off it starts only once it cools down; code P1570 (immobilizer lockout). The culprit was the immobilizer antenna amplifier: chilled in a freezer, it worked. After replacement it starts hot too.

Driver assistance warnings now and then, more than 20 codes stored. After clearing, only B2D04 remained — front camera circuit: the connector latch was broken. We repaired the connector; recheck the rest after a few days of driving.

The revs hunt, the engine stalls now and then, code P0368. No air leak, but the code came back right after clearing. We recommended checking the camshaft sensor, its connector, wiring, power and ground, as well as the timing marks.

Won’t start after a fuel filter replacement. On this model the pump runs only while cranking, not with the ignition on — power was normal. The pump is fine; the new filter turned out to be defective and leaking.
Check Engine and ABS, fuel smell on start-up; P04567A — very small EVAP leak. The purge valve worked, no major leak. Tip: replace the fuel cap first; if the code comes back — the purge valve.

Unstable idle, misfires, about fifteen codes stored. After cleaning and adapting the throttle body the idle became steadier; next we recommended the spark plugs, HT leads, O2 sensors, EVAP, MAF sensor and a search for air leaks.

Starts cold, but once warm the starter won’t turn until it cools down. The battery, terminals, ignition switch and starter are fine — the starter relay stopped engaging after heating up. After the relay was replaced, it starts hot too.

Cranks but won’t start; code U0100 — lost communication with the engine control module. The cause was corroded wiring that disrupted power and communication with the ECU. We repaired that section and cleaned the contacts — it started, communication is back.
Stumbling, vibration at idle, slow to rev up; diagnostics showed misfires, other parameters normal. After a new set of spark plugs the engine runs smoothly, no codes.

The fan runs all the time, active code P011600 — implausible temperature sensor signal. The sensor readings are normal — the contacts in its connector had corroded. We cleaned the contacts, the fan works as it should, and the sensor wasn’t replaced.

Runs unevenly and stalls while driving: P0304, P0303, P0300, P0363. The spark plugs show burn marks and two have cracked ceramic; the coils and boots are intact. We recommended replacing the plug set with catalog-specified ones and rechecking.

An imported car starts, but the automatic transmission’s rotary selector dial doesn’t work — it can’t be driven; no codes. Under the hood the transport mode latch wasn’t in the operating position — we moved it back and the dial worked.

The cooling fan runs constantly, no codes. The fan control module is under the left headlight: with its connector unplugged the fan started working normally — we recommended replacing the fan control module.

Misfires and rough running, but no codes stored. The misfire counters in the live data pointed to cylinders 1 and 4. The plugs fitted weren’t the catalog ones — first we recommended replacing them with the correct ones.

Check Engine is on, but it drives as usual: P02CB00 and P029900 — low boost pressure, U115800 — left air flap. Too early to replace the turbos: first the air filters, intake and flap, then a repeat diagnosis.

Fails the inspection on CO, no obvious complaints; code B279A is unrelated, and the sensors show no critical deviations. We cleaned the MAF sensor and throttle body and ran an adaptation; if CO stays high — check the fuel system.
Check Engine on an almost new car, code P24507E — EVAP system. A hands-on inspection found a mechanically damaged canister — probably from loading or shipping. Replacement or repair is recommended.

Check Engine, Traction and ABS are on. The engine has P0037 — B1S2 oxygen sensor heater circuit; the ABS module has no codes: Traction is on because of the engine code. We recommended checking the heater circuit and the sensor.

Check Engine on, code P217700 — lean mixture off idle. Given the 74 000 km mileage, we recommended checking and, if needed, replacing the fuel filter and checking the injectors, rather than replacing parts based on a single code.

After the battery voltage dropped, it stopped recognizing the key; the spare key didn’t help either. We synchronized the immobilizer and ECU — key recognition was restored, the engine started, and no new key was needed.

Stopped starting right after the key battery was replaced. When the key was taken apart, the immobilizer chip fell out of the housing and got lost. We fitted a new chip and paired it to the factory immobilizer — the engine started.
Wouldn’t start after sitting for a long time in winter; after many attempts the battery went completely flat. On site we warmed the car up and supplied power for cranking — the car started.

Wouldn’t start after a few hours parked in the frost. A jump-start didn’t help: the starter was getting power but the engine wouldn’t fire — it wasn’t just the battery. After warming it up on site, it started without a tow truck.

Limp mode, no faster than 20 km/h: active P3822 (low AdBlue concentration), P1518, P151A. We cleared the codes and ran an adaptation — the restriction is lifted; AdBlue quality and concentration still need checking.

Neither heater fan works, and the fuse blows even with the fans disconnected. When they were last replaced, the wires got pinched — the insulation chafed through and shorted to ground. We repaired the wiring and the heater works.

The diesel won’t start; after clearing, P2951 (injection pump metering unit) came back. The oil is too thin and there are signs of an air leak. We recommended checking the injection pump, fuel pressure, oil and compression, and not starting it until then.

After replacing the flywheel-driven pump, the engine stalls at exactly 1200 rpm when revving up smoothly. Through the inspection window we found three bent flywheel teeth — replacing the flywheel and checking the crankshaft sensor is recommended.

Stalled while driving with an almost empty tank and wouldn’t start after refueling; stored codes 2045-001 (crankshaft sensor) and 2017-001 (low rail pressure). It started on the second try — there was probably air in the system, and the fuel got primed through.

The engine won’t shut off after the ignition is turned off; the recent starter repair was suspected. The culprit is a worn ignition switch: the key comes out before the switch reaches the off position. The switch had been repaired more than once — it needs replacing.

After a water pump replacement, cooling system codes; after clearing, DTC 5864 remained — coolant level sensor, loose contact: check the connector and wiring. Trailer turn signal codes while the turn signals work — check the bulb ratings.

Mileage 5 000 km, temperature and thermostat codes (P1000, P0115, P07CB) and others; after clearing, most didn’t come back. The AdBlue warning was just a low urea level: it went away after topping up. While we were at it, we switched the instrument cluster to Russian.

Seven codes after an engine repair; after clearing, 1117 remained, and 0778 appeared while cranking — camshaft sensor, erratic signal. We recommended checking the timing marks, the reluctor teeth and the mechanical parts.

The fan clutch won’t engage and the engine overheats; code 23770 — fan control circuit. We found a defect in the fan clutch connector — after repairing it the clutch engages and the overheating is gone.

The transmission stopped shifting properly. After clearing, code 3248 remained — clutch actuator B385, position initialization. Conclusion: most likely the mechanics of the clutch actuator or the gearbox; after the repair — an initialization.

The engine won’t rev above 1500 rpm, limp mode; SPN 520359 FMI 31 — open circuit in the pressure control valve circuit. The wire had chafed against the conduit — we repaired it with solder and secured the harness; the revs came back.

Won’t start, code P1065 — ECCS main relay circuit. The relay and power supply are fine — the wiring in the relay control circuit was damaged, so the module couldn’t switch on system power. We repaired the wiring and it started.

The engine is misfiring and has lost power, code SPN 653 — injector control circuit. The cause was a damaged contact in the injector connector. We repinned the connector and cleared the codes — the engine runs smoothly and the power is back.

Won’t start: after the fuel was changed and bled, diesel doesn’t come out of the injection pump. The injection pump’s pressure relief valve had stuck open — we removed it, cleaned it, freed it up with careful tapping and bled the system — it started.

The battery was completely dead: the fob and central locking wouldn’t open the car, and the mechanical key didn’t open the door either. We supplied external power through an accessible part of the power circuit — the central locking opened the car with no damage.

Check Engine came on before a trip to Astana. A stored code 71-8 — glow plug relay, short or open circuit. After clearing, the codes didn’t return and the engine ran normally — nothing standing in the way of the trip.

Clouds of black smoke and loss of power while driving. Codes SPN 4364 FMI 15 (SCR), SPN 729 FMI 5 and SPN 158 FMI 2 don’t explain this fault. We recommended diesel injection specialists: check the injectors and the fuel system.

Black smoke and uneven running; codes 285, 3326, 6263, 559, 2311, 272 — mostly Inactive, didn’t return after clearing. Commanded and actual Common Rail pressure matched; checking the injectors and fuel injection system is recommended.

Pre-purchase inspection, stated mileage about 400 000 km. After clearing and starting, AdBlue, fuel system and parking heater codes came back, and the module data showed over 1 000 000 km — the buyer decided not to buy.

Pre-purchase inspection, mileage 3 500 km. Current GSM/GPS lock codes (U016AF7, U016AF3) came back after clearing — we advised the buyer to demand they be fixed before the deal. The VIN and mileage matched.

After an engine wash, water got into the ECU: corrosion damaged the board’s traces and vias. We restored the board and sealed the unit — the engine started. Tip: don’t wash the engine with a pressurized water jet.

The ECU doesn’t communicate and the engine won’t start. A solder joint under the BGA processor had lost contact — the unit sits on hardened anti-vibration bushings. We reballed the processor: communication came back and the engine started.

The engine misfires and the ignition coil keeps burning out. The coil driver transistor in the ECU had failed — replacing the coil alone won’t fix it. We repaired and sealed the unit, and the misfire stopped.
The alarm is blocking the start
Disarm the car with the fob again, try the second fob, and replace the fob battery.
Find the Valet button — usually under the steering wheel, by the fuse box or under the dash: turn the ignition on and press it several times.
Check the fuses, the battery terminals and whether any connectors have come loose.
If the starter won’t crank, it’s most likely the alarm blocking it; if it starts with the key but not with remote start, it’s the immobilizer.
If the fuel pump isn’t running, don’t rush to buy a new one: the alarm may be cutting power to the pump.
Codes in many modules at once, or no communication with a module
Write the codes down, clear them and check again: after a flat battery, a repair or voltage spikes, codes that are no longer current stay in memory.
If there was off-roading, body work or front-end disassembly before this, inspect the connectors and their latches: one poorly seated or broken connector causes codes in many modules.
Check the fuses and power supply of the module that isn’t communicating.

If you have a multimeter, measure the CAN resistance at the OBD port between CAN-H and CAN-L with the ignition off and the battery disconnected: about 60 Ω is normal, 120 Ω means one line is open, 0–10 Ω means a short.
Think back to whether an alarm or GPS tracker was installed: a poor installation often breaks the CAN bus.
ABS light is on
Check the ABS fuses.
Inspect the ABS sensor connectors at the wheels for corrosion and the wiring near the wheels for damage.
Make sure the battery isn’t flat: the code can also come from a voltage dip or a bad ground.
If the code appeared after a car wash or rain, dry out the connectors and plugs.
If Check Engine is on along with ABS, read the engine codes first: on a Lexus RX350, Traction and ABS came on because of P0037, while the ABS module had no codes.
EVAP code or fuel smell
With a small-leak code, start with the fuel cap: its seal loses tightness over time.
Inspect the system hoses for cracks, and check the connectors, especially the one on the purge valve.
Listen for the purge valve clicking, and check for a fuel smell under the hood.
Think back to whether the tank was filled right up to the neck: that harms the canister.
If the car has been in a collision or was recently delivered, inspect the canister, lines and hoses for mechanical damage.
Temperature gauge jumping: check the temperature sensor
Inspect the temperature sensor connector: look for corrosion, a broken wire or a loose contact.
Check whether the sensor itself is turning in its housing: that kind of mechanical defect has caused jumping readings.
With a scan tool: on a cold engine the temperature is about the same as the air temperature and rises smoothly as it warms up; −40 °C or +130 °C means a faulty sensor or wiring.
The connector should have power (usually 5 V) and ground; no power means a problem in the wiring or the ECU.
Don’t rush to replace the thermostat: first the sensor, its connector and its readings in the live data.
Won’t start after rain or a car wash
Dry out the ignition coils and spark plug wells, and check the leads for arcing.
Look inside the underhood fuse box for water; check the fuses and relays and dry the box out.
Check the main connectors — ECU, sensors, relays — and clean any corroded contacts.
Clean and tighten the battery terminals, check the charge, and see whether there’s water in the air filter.
From now on, don’t wash the engine with a pressure washer or a strong jet: water in the ECU corrodes the board, sometimes not right away.
If it stalls after 1–3 seconds and the key symbol flashes, try the second key: that’s how the immobilizer blocks it.
Check the fuses and listen for whether the fuel pump runs.
Inspect the plugs and connectors, and check the battery and terminals.
If it started after a battery terminal was disconnected, the cause may be a dirty throttle plate: it needs cleaning and adaptation.
If it started after a throttle body cleaning or other intake work, check that all the hoses and pipes are in place.
The car won’t rev up
Look at Check Engine: if it won’t rev above 2500–3000 rpm and the light is on, that’s limp mode — the codes need reading.
Check the air filter and the fuel level.
Check how the engine responds to the gas pedal.
If it drives but feels weak, you can drive on carefully; if there are jerks, misfiring or a power limit, better not to risk it.
If it misfires and accelerates poorly, start with the spark plugs: on the RAV4 2008 a new set of plugs solved everything.
Diesel: black smoke and loss of power
If it jerked while driving, put out thick black smoke and stalled, don’t try to restart it until it’s checked: a faulty injector can damage the engine.
Check the oil: if it’s too thin or shows signs of diesel, don’t start the engine until the cause is found.
No codes doesn’t mean the engine is healthy: with black smoke, the injectors and fuel injection system need checking by diesel specialists.
If you have a scan tool, compare the commanded and actual rail pressure; a match still doesn’t rule out faulty injectors.
Won’t start in the cold
Don’t crank the starter for long or many times in a row: the battery will go completely flat, and warming up alone won’t be enough.
If you’ve jump-started it and the starter cranks normally but the engine won’t catch, it’s not just the battery: there’s no point in jump-starting over and over.
If it regularly struggles to start already at −10…−15 °C, check the battery, the spark or glow plugs, the fuel supply and the oil viscosity.
Warming the car up on the spot often helps — a tow truck usually isn’t needed.
Car won’t open: dead battery
Take the mechanical key out of the fob: press the release button and pull it out.
Open the driver’s door with it: the lock cylinder is often hidden under a decorative cap on the handle.
Once it’s open, open the hood and charge or jump-start the battery.
Don’t open it with a wire or a screwdriver and don’t bend the door: you’ll damage the lock, the seals or the window regulator.
If the key didn’t open the lock, the car can be opened by supplying external power to the power circuit, but that takes experience: better call a technician.
Rear window defroster not working
Turn the defroster on: if the whole window stays cold, there’s no power; if it heats in stripes, some grid lines are broken.
Check the defroster fuse.
Inspect the contacts and connectors along the edges of the glass and clean off any corrosion.
Find the break: turn the defroster on and carefully run your hand over the glass — the cold spot is where the break is; the lines are repaired with conductive glue.
On wagons and hatchbacks, check the wiring in the tailgate for breaks.
Parking heater not working
Check the battery charge, terminals and ground: a parking heater is very sensitive to voltage.
Inspect the parking heater fuses and check the power at the heater.
Check that there’s fuel and listen for whether the fuel pump runs.
After a fuel change or a long period of disuse, the system sometimes has to be primed with several starts in a row.
After several failed starts some parking heaters lock out — they need unlocking through diagnostics.
A/C not cooling
Don’t rush to recharge the refrigerant: in Oleg’s experience, in Almaty the cause is electrical in 40–50 % of cases.
Check the A/C fuse and relay.
Press A/C and listen for the compressor clicking on.
Check whether the cooling fan spins with the A/C on.
Inspect the connectors for corrosion and the ground on the body.
Transmission selector dial won’t rise or turn
Check the battery charge: with low voltage the dial may not rise.
Press the brake pedal: if the system doesn’t see the pedal, the dial won’t unlock.
Check the fuses and switch the ignition off and on again.
If the car was recently shipped in, check the transport mode latch under the hood: on the Evoque it wasn’t in the operating position.
Don’t force the dial and don’t apply power directly — you could burn out the module.
How to check an O2 sensor
Inspect the sensor wires and connector for damage, corrosion or soot.
With a scan tool: the signal should “jump around”; if it’s “frozen” or keeps showing the same value, the sensor is faulty.
With a multimeter on a warm engine the signal swings from about 0,1 to 0,9 V; if it doesn’t change, the sensor isn’t working.
With a heater circuit code like P0037, check the sensor’s connectors and heater circuit before replacing it.
Don’t replace the sensor right away: the cause can be an air leak, the MAF sensor, the fuel system or misfires.
Alarm goes off by itself
Check the battery: when the voltage dips, the alarm goes off falsely, especially at night and in winter.
Inspect the door, hood and trunk switches.
Try lowering the shock sensor sensitivity.
Check the terminals for corrosion; if it started after rain, there’s most likely moisture in the sensors or wiring.
Don’t put it off: often the alarm starts acting up first, and then the car stops starting.
The alarm can block the starter, ignition or fuel pump — then the car won’t start even though everything else is fine. You can often disarm it yourself.
The scan tool shows codes in many modules at once (U codes) or can’t see a particular module. Most often it’s not the modules themselves but power, ground, connectors and the CAN bus wiring.
The ABS light is on, often together with Traction or ESP. The usual cause is a wheel speed sensor, its connector or wiring; less often, low voltage or a code from another module.
Check Engine is on with a fuel vapor recovery system (EVAP) code, or there’s a fuel smell. The system is sealed; the module notices even a tiny leak.
The temperature gauge jumps around even though the engine warms up normally. Often the culprit is the temperature sensor or its connector, not the thermostat.
After rain or a car wash, water gets onto the coils, spark plugs and connectors and into the fuse box — the engine won’t start or misfires.
The engine starts and stalls after a couple of seconds. The cause can be the immobilizer, the fuel supply, the throttle body or a bad contact.
The engine runs, but the car won’t rev up or accelerates poorly. If Check Engine is on as well, the module may have switched to limp mode.
The diesel puts out black smoke, loses power or stalls while driving. A common cause is the injectors or fuel injection system, and there may be no codes at all.
In the cold the engine won’t start or the starter barely turns. The main thing is not to run the battery completely flat.
With a dead battery the fob and central locking don’t work and the car won’t open. Almost every fob has a mechanical key hidden inside.
The rear window defroster doesn’t heat at all or heats in stripes.
The parking heater won’t start or goes out right away. A parking heater is very sensitive to voltage and fuel supply.
The A/C blows warm. Before recharging the refrigerant, check the electrics: fuse, relay, compressor and fan.
The gear selector dial won’t rise or turn — the car won’t let you select a gear.
How to check an O2 sensor yourself — with a scan tool and a multimeter — before replacing it.
The alarm goes off on its own — at night, in rain or in the cold. Most often the culprits are low voltage, the pin switches or the shock sensor.
After a car has been rebuilt, especially after body work or front-end disassembly, it’s important to carefully check all electrical connectors, the wiring and that the plugs are locked in.
After off-road trips, the cause of many codes is often not the electronic modules but mechanical damage to the wiring and connectors.
If a fault shows up again right after the codes are cleared, it most often means there’s a real fault.

Won’t turn on at all, the controller is dark
Controller lights up, but the pump doesn’t tick

Error code on the controller or a flashing light
Parking heater won’t turn on at all
The controller stays dark and doesn’t respond to buttons: power isn’t reaching the heater or the controller, or there’s no connection between them.
Check the battery charge and terminals: at low voltage the heater’s control unit won’t switch on or shuts off right away.
Find the parking heater fuses: they’re usually in a separate holder on the power lead near the battery or near the heater itself, not in the car’s fuse box.
Inspect the positive and ground at the heater and the harness connectors: corrosion and wires chafed under the floor are a common cause.
Check the controller wire and connector. If the controller has a clock or timer, check that its settings haven’t been reset.
On a truck, check the battery isolator switch: on many vehicles the parking heater won’t work without it.
If the controller lights up but shows a communication error or flashes, find the code below.
The parking heater starts — the controller is lit and the fan spins — but the fuel pump doesn’t tick, and the heater shuts down with an error.
Wait a moment: the pump doesn’t start ticking straight away, only once the glow plug (glow pin) has heated up, a while after switching on.
Check the connector on the fuel pump and the wires to it: the pump sits under the floor or near the tank, and its connector often corrodes.

Check whether pulses reach the pump: connect an LED test light to the pump connector — during start-up it should flash in rhythm. If it flashes but the pump is silent, the pump is faulty. If it doesn’t flash, look at the wiring or the heater’s control unit.
In winter, summer diesel thickens and clogs the thin fuel line and the pump: fill up with winter diesel and warm the line and pump in a heated garage.
Check the fuel level: the heater’s fuel pickup is usually shorter than the main one, so with only a little fuel left in the tank the heater gets none.
After a long idle period or a pump replacement, the system is primed with several starts in a row; many models have a priming mode for this — see the manual.
Outside the season, manufacturers advise running the parking heater briefly once a month so the pump and the fan motor don’t seize up.
After switching on you can’t hear the fan (blower), or the heater shuts off without purging.
Right after switching on, the fan should start spinning. If you hear nothing at all, start with power: battery, the parking heater fuses, ground.
Inspect the heater’s air intake and exhaust pipe: snow, ice, dirt or leaves hinder both the fan and combustion.
If the fan hums but won’t spin, or spins in jerks, the bearing has seized or the motor is worn. Don’t force the impeller round — it breaks easily. The blower needs repair or replacement.

The purge after switching off is essential: it cools the combustion chamber and the glow plug. Don’t cut power or ground while the heater is purging — that is the most common reason glow plugs burn out and soot builds up.
If the fan spins but no warm air comes out, check the air duct: kinks, crushing, closed flaps.
Parking heater starts and then goes out
The heater starts working but doesn’t light properly or goes out after a few minutes, often with an error code.
Check the battery: during start-up the glow plug (glow pin) draws a lot of current, and with a weak battery the control unit aborts the start.
Check the fuel supply: is the pump ticking, is there enough fuel, has the diesel thickened in the frost.
Inspect the air intake and exhaust pipe: a crushed or blocked pipe, snow or dirt prevent proper combustion.
After several failed starts in a row many parking heaters lock out and show a lockout error. How to clear it is in the model’s manual or done through diagnostics.
A sooted or open-circuit glow plug (glow pin), a clogged evaporator mesh, soot in the combustion chamber — that’s a repair for a technician: it needs dismantling and cleaning.
Parking heater smokes
A little smoke during the first seconds of start-up and during the purge after switching off is normal. If it smokes all the time, combustion is off.
If you smell exhaust or see smoke inside the cabin, switch the heater off at once and air out: carbon monoxide is deadly. Don’t switch it on again until it’s repaired.
Black smoke and soot mean more fuel than the air can burn: check the air intake and exhaust pipe (crushing, dirt, snow), then soot in the combustion chamber.
White smoke smelling of diesel means the fuel isn’t burning: a weak glow plug (glow pin), a clogged evaporator mesh or bad fuel — summer diesel in winter, fuel with water or mixed with petrol.
If smoke comes not from the exhaust pipe but from under the casing or into the air duct, the heat exchanger or a gasket has burned through. Don’t switch the heater on; repair only at a technician.
Cleaning the combustion chamber and replacing gaskets is a job for a technician: the heater has to be dismantled.
Error code on the parking heater controller
Choose the heater’s make and model and enter the code — I’ll show what it means and what to do.
Write down the code from the controller or count the flashes: the light usually flashes in series with a pause, and the number of flashes in a series is the error number.
You can usually clear the error by switching the heater off and on again. If the error comes back, find the cause — otherwise after several attempts the heater locks out.

How to switch the head unit and instrument cluster to Russian
Russian is often already in the menu — it’s just hard to find when everything is in another language. Look for the icons and words below.
On the head unit, open the settings: the gear icon, the SETUP, MENU or Settings button. On a Chinese screen it’s 设置, on a Japanese one 設定, on a Korean one 설정.
Find the language item: Language, in Chinese 语言, in Japanese 言語, in Korean 언어. It’s often inside the System or General section: System, General, 系统, 通用, システム, 일반.
Choose «Русский» (Russian). If there’s no Russian but English is available, set English for now.
On many cars the cluster takes its language from the head unit: after changing the language, switch the ignition off and on again.
If the cluster hasn’t switched, open its menu with the steering wheel buttons (arrows and OK, or the gear icon): Settings → Language.
If the head unit supports CarPlay or Android Auto, connect your phone: maps, music and calls will be in your phone’s language.
This happens with cars built for the Japanese, Korean, Chinese and US markets: the head unit or cluster software has no Russian.
Set English if it’s available — it’s easier to follow while you sort things out.
Connect your phone via CarPlay or Android Auto: maps, music and calls will be in your phone’s language even if the head unit menu is in another language.
If this model is officially sold in Kazakhstan, ask the official dealer: sometimes there’s an official update with Russian for it.

The head unit can be replaced with another one that fits in size and connectors. Check in advance that the camera, steering wheel buttons and car settings (if they are on this screen) will keep working.
Don’t install unofficial “Russification” patches or firmware: the unit may stop turning on, and you can lose features and the warranty.
A cluster from another version of the car is fitted only by a technician and only keeping the real mileage: rewriting the mileage is not allowed.
A car from the US or the UK shows speed and mileage in miles.
Look in the cluster or head unit settings: the Units, Distance or Units of measure item. On many cars you can choose km and km/h there.
An analogue speedometer on American cars usually has a second km/h scale in small figures inside the main one.
Conversion: 1 mile is 1.609 km; 60 mph is about 97 km/h; 100,000 miles is about 161,000 km.
If it can’t be switched in the settings, the cluster is reconfigured by a technician or dealer. The mileage must stay real: rewriting it is not allowed.
Connection to the car over Ethernet (DoIP) via the computer

Newer cars with DoIP (BMW, VW, Mercedes, Volvo, Jaguar Land Rover): an ENET cable into the computer’s network port, or a Scanmatik 3 — the “ENET / Ethernet (DoIP)” item. The Scanmatik 3 also connects over CAN FD — on its own, after classic CAN.

Works with an inexpensive ELM327 and with Scanmatik via a computer. Scanmatik reads and clears codes, shows live data, module tests, readiness monitors, mileage and engine hours, and runs service checks. We never write to modules.
Codes and clearing them, live data, module tests, readiness monitors, mileage and engine hours, service checks — nothing is written to the control units.
How to jump-start a car properly
Jump-starting is safe if you keep to the order of the cables. Reversed polarity or a spark at the battery can burn out control units, and battery gas can ignite.
Don’t jump a swollen, cracked or frozen battery and don’t lean over it — it can explode. A hybrid or EV is jumped only through its 12 V battery, following the owner’s manual.
Park the cars close, but not touching. Switch off the donor’s engine, and turn off the ignition and everything unnecessary in both cars.
Check the voltage: 12 V is jumped only from 12 V, and 24 V only from 24 V.
Red cable: first to the positive of the flat battery, then to the donor’s positive.
Black cable: first to the donor’s negative, then to clean, unpainted metal on your car’s engine, away from the battery. Not to the flat battery’s negative: a spark at the battery is dangerous.
If the battery is in the boot or under a seat, there are usually jump terminals under the bonnet: a positive post under a cover and a ground bolt.
A jump starter (booster) is connected the same way: red to positive, black to engine ground, and only then switched on.
Start the donor and let it run for 5–10 minutes: the flat battery will take a little charge.
Start your car: crank no longer than 10 seconds, with a 30-second pause between attempts. If it won’t start after 3–4 attempts, don’t torture the starter — the cause may not be the battery.
Once it starts, remove the cables in reverse order: black from your car, black from the donor, red from the donor, red from your car. The cable ends must not touch each other or the body.
A drive won’t fully recharge the battery: charge it with a charger and find out why it went flat — the button below.
A 24 V truck is jumped from 24 V. The battery isolator on the flat vehicle must be switched on.
How to tell the battery is worn out
A battery usually lasts 3–5 years. An old one may show normal voltage with no load but sag when it cranks the starter.
Look for the manufacturing date on the case or label: older than 4–5 years is already a reason to test it.
Measure the resting voltage 1–2 hours after a drive, with everything off: 12.6–12.8 V is charged, about 12.4 V is roughly 75 %, 12.2 V is half, 12.0 V and below is flat.
Cranking test: have a helper crank the starter while you watch the voltmeter. A healthy battery stays at 9.5–10 V or above; lower means it’s weak or flat.
Charge the battery with a charger and test again: if the voltage drops quickly or the starter cranks slowly again, it’s time to replace the battery.
A swollen case, cracks or electrolyte leaks — replace it at once.
A load tester or battery analyser check can be done at a battery shop or by an auto electrician.
Choose the new battery to match the original’s capacity, cold-cranking current and polarity. On cars with start-stop, use only the same type, AGM or EFB.
On many newer cars (BMW, Audi, VW, Mercedes and others) a new battery is registered with a scan tool — otherwise the car will charge it incorrectly.
On 24 V there are two batteries: measure each separately and replace them as a pair — a new one paired with an old one soon fails.
Flat because the lights were left on
If the battery went flat once because the lights or the radio were left on, there’s no current drain — but the battery needs a full charge.
Jump-start the car — the cable order is in the “How to jump-start a car properly” tip.
A 20–30 minute drive won’t fully recharge the battery: charge it with a charger.
Deep discharge harms the battery, and in winter a flat battery can freeze. Don’t leave the car out in the frost with a flat battery.
A day after charging, measure the resting voltage: 12.6 V or more is fine. Below 12.4 V means the battery is weak or there’s a current drain.
